Issue Reading note
The record stops one week before the next print Q1 2026 is the last reported quarter. Q2 2026 reports 5 August 2026 and contains, at once, the first Foundayo revenue quarter, the first full quarter of the (25)% ex-US price reset, the first month under Medicare obesity access, and a guidance update. Every FY2026 figure here has a one-week shelf life.
Franchise profitability does not exist in the disclosure Lilly reports one segment with the CEO as chief operating decision maker measuring consolidated net income. No cost of sales, R&D, marketing or capital is allocated to therapeutic areas. Every franchise margin, ROIC or unit cost in this document is an [estimate] with its method and bounds attached, or an explicit gap.
Three FY2025 EPS figures circulate, all correct Reported GAAP $22.95; Lilly's own non-GAAP $24.21 (which does not exclude acquired in-process R&D); bonus-plan adjusted non-GAAP $27.06 (which does). A trailing P/E on FY2025 is 46.8x, 44.4x or 39.2x depending on the denominator. Every multiple below states its basis.
Two revenue lines contain divestiture gains FY2023 revenue includes a $1.4bn net gain on the olanzapine portfolio sale and $579M on Baqsimi; FY2025 "Other" includes $180M on the ex-US Cialis rights sale. Lilly books gains on product-rights sales as revenue, not other income, so the FY2023-to-FY2024 neuroscience decline is largely an accounting artefact.

Product-level disclosure narrowed sharply in FY2025: the 10-K's product table now names only Mounjaro, Zepbound and Verzenio, and Cyramza, Erbitux, Tyvyt, Retevmo, Olumiant, Emgality, Humalog, Humulin and Basaglar lost their separate revenue lines. Lilly discloses no units, prescriptions or patients for any product, so the unit economics below are triangulated from IQVIA charts in Lilly's own decks, published list prices and CMS Part D files. The session's web-search budget was exhausted before several late verifications could be completed; claims that could not be re-fetched are tagged [web, unverified].

1. Business description, model and unit economics

Lilly discovers, manufactures and sells prescription medicines in five therapeutic groupings. It reports one segment, so the groupings below are the Note 2 revenue disaggregation, not reported business units.

Franchise FY2025 revenue % of total YoY FY2025 YoY FY2024 YoY FY2023 What it sells
Incretin (Mounjaro, Zepbound) $36,508M 56.0% +122% +208% n/m One molecule, tirzepatide, under two brands: weekly injectable dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist for type 2 diabetes and for obesity
Established cardiometabolic $11,713M 18.0% (10)% (9)% +2% Trulicity, a share of Boehringer Ingelheim's Jardiance sales, and the insulins
Oncology $9,376M 14.4% +7% +32% +18% Verzenio plus six smaller brands; specialist-prescribed, 70% oral
Immunology $5,247M 8.1% +19% +16% +14% Taltz, Olumiant, Ebglyss, Omvoh; retail biologics under PBM formulary control
Neuroscience and other $2,334M 3.6% (2)% (41)% (21)% Kisunla, Emgality, and an unnamed legacy residual
Total $65,179M 100% +45% +32% +20%

The FY2023 neuroscience decline and the FY2024 comparison are distorted by the $1.4bn olanzapine gain booked as 2023 revenue (10-K FY2025 Note 3).

One molecule is the company. Tirzepatide revenue went from $483M in 2022 to $36,508M in 2025 and 64.8% of Q1 2026 revenue. Everything else Lilly sells produced $28,058M in 2022 and $28,672M in 2025, a compound rate of 0.7% a year. Tirzepatide supplied 98.3% of the three-year revenue increase, 99.5% of the FY2025 increase and 94.3% of the Q1 2026 increase▪ (10-K FY2025 Note 2; 10-Q 2026-Q1 Note 2).

1.1 The incretin revenue equation

Lilly discloses revenue by product by geography and a company-level split of revenue change into volume, realized price and foreign exchange. It discloses no units. The unit used throughout is a 28-day script — four weekly doses, one patient-month — because it is what the payer pays for, what the self-pay consumer buys, what IQVIA counts, and what a management-confirmed price arithmetic exists for.

On the Q1 2026 call an analyst put the calculation to management directly: about 7.0 million US Zepbound prescriptions against $4,134M of US Zepbound revenue implies roughly $580 per prescription, or about $550 after normalising a one-time rebate adjustment. The CFO answered "your math is pretty spot on, by the way" (Q1 2026 earnings call, Q&A). That anchor, plus the IQVIA prescription series on Lilly's own deck slide 9, gives two independent routes to volume that agree.

Mounjaro — US ~9.0M [estimate: deck IQVIA market × disclosed 60.1% Lilly share, less Zepbound and Trulicity] ~$470 [estimate: $4,232M ÷ derived scripts] ~$65 ~$405 ~86% Revenue: 10-Q 2026-Q1 Note 2

The per-unit build reconciles to reported cost of sales. FY2025 franchise scripts of 70–84M at about $60 each implies franchise cost of sales of $4,200M–$5,040M against reported consolidated cost of sales of $11,052M; the residual implies a non-incretin gross margin of 76%–79%, consistent with a book of Trulicity, insulins, Verzenio, Taltz and a Jardiance collaboration share.▪ A second, independent method — solving the two-period mix system across FY2024 and FY2025 — gives an incretin gross margin of 86.9% against the bottom-up 86%. The two agree within a point. [estimate: mix algebra holding the non-incretin book at its FY2023 79.2% gross margin; range 84%–89%]

Cost per script is almost entirely absorbed fixed cost. Peptide active ingredient plus device is a small single-digit share of the $60–70 per script; published cost-based work on injectable semaglutide puts production plus logistics, tax and a 50% margin under $5 a month, and tirzepatide is a longer peptide at higher loading, so that figure is directional rather than transferable (JAMA Network Open 2024, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. The balance is fill-finish, release, freight and the absorbed cost of a manufacturing estate still under construction. The consequence is that marginal gross margin on an incremental script is far above the ~86% average, which is why cutting the LillyDirect price from $499 to $299–449 still grows gross profit dollars, and why the binding constraint is demand-side rather than cost.▪

Operating leverage: Lilly's income statement has no operating-income subtotal; it runs from revenue to income before income taxes. Constructing operating income as revenue less cost of sales, R&D and marketing/selling/administrative, and excluding acquired IPR&D:

$M FY2021 FY2022 FY2023 FY2024 FY2025 Q1 2026
Constructed operating income 7,643 8,280 10,325 17,040 29,696 9,778
Margin 27.0% 29.0% 30.3% 37.8% 45.6% 49.4%
Δ operating income / Δ revenue — n/m 36.6% 61.5% 62.9% 63.3%

Cumulative FY2022–FY2025 incremental margin is 58.5%. Because the incretin franchise supplied 99.5% of FY2025 revenue growth, that realized 63% is, to a first approximation, the franchise's incremental margin after paying for the R&D and commercial infrastructure of the whole company.▪

1.2 Demand-driver decomposition

Management's stated driver is penetration of the eligible obese population — "mid-single digits" in the US, "something like 1%" globally (Q4 2025 call; Ricks at Bernstein, 2026-05-28). That is a demand ceiling, not a driver. Decomposed to what actually moves volume:

Driver Ultimate exposure, measurably Contribution Robustness Did it show up in the realized record?
US reimbursed volume The annual employer opt-in decision on an anti-obesity rider, the CMS Part D coverage window, state Medicaid line items, and PBM template formularies. Not obesity prevalence ~55% of US Zepbound scripts and effectively all US Mounjaro scripts; roughly 60–65% of franchise revenue Structural per covered patient, but the coverage vote is re-taken every plan year and can be revoked No. Commercial access has been "pretty steady around 50%" for at least a year (Yuffa, Q1 2026 call) while franchise revenue roughly doubled. CVS Caremark's July 2025 formulary removal cost about 2 points of US branded-obesity prescription share; California's Medicaid withdrawal cost "high single digits" of Q1 2026 prescription growth
US self-pay volume US household discretionary spending at $299–$449 a month, against a competitive floor set by Novo's cash-pay pricing and by compounded or foreign generic semaglutide Self-pay went from ~5% of US Zepbound scripts in Q4 2024 to ~45% in Q1 2026, and from low teens to 55% of new prescriptions Secular in direction but price-elastic, with no precedent. Ricks: "I am hard-pressed to think of an analog where you have this many people paying out of pocket for a prescription medication" (Q4 2025 call) Yes. This is the demonstrated driver. It went from roughly zero to 45% of scripts in six quarters while commercial access sat still
Ex-US volume National formulary listing votes — China's NRDL, European HTA bodies, Japan's NHI — and, where there is no listing, ex-US self-pay (about 75% of the ex-US Mounjaro book) 34.6% of franchise revenue in Q1 2026, up from 25.5% in FY2025; 49% of the franchise's Q1 2026 growth dollars Structural where listed; the concession is permanent Yes, and accelerating. Ex-US Mounjaro grew 273% year over year in Q1 2026. Jonsson concedes share gain is largely done: above 53% ex-US, "incremental share gain is getting harder"
Net price per script Channel mix, negotiated government prices, and the per-channel rebate rate Price contributed +4pp (2023), +5pp (2024), (6)pp (2025), (13)pp (Q1 2026) to revenue growth; guided to a low-to-mid-teens decline for FY2026 Structural, one-way and partly contractual. The November 2025 US government agreements, the China NRDL listing and the Medicaid most-favoured-nation mechanism are not reversible Yes, in the opposite direction from the 2023–24 experience. The 2023 and 2024 price increases were a gross-to-net repair — the FY2023 10-K attributes them to "decreased utilization of savings card programs as access continued to expand" — and a coupon burn-off runs once

The covered-channel price rose while the blended price declined. Solving the Zepbound US script price into its two channels using the CFO-confirmed blended price and the disclosed self-pay mix: covered-channel net revenue per script was roughly $630 in Q1 2025 and roughly $673 in Q1 2026 (range $632–$714 across a $350–$450 self-pay realization), while the blended figure declined from about $607 to $550 normalized.▪ [estimate: disclosed blended price, disclosed channel mix, solved for the residual] The CFO's own framing supports this only with a carve-out: prices "have been relatively stable quarter-on-quarter" after removing the most-favoured-nation agreement and the NRDL listing. Ricks added a correction the arithmetic does not capture — "there is a reasonable amount of medical exception and OSA usage that moves across channels at close to an undiscounted price" — and neither he nor the CFO sized that share.

Gross-to-net reductions are larger than reported US revenue. US rebates, discounts and returns reduced net sales by $62,135M in 2025 against $43,481M of reported US revenue, implying US gross sales of $105,616M▪ and a 58.8% US gross-to-net reduction, against 43.1% in 2016. The roll-forward covers only Lilly's most significant US programmes, so that is a lower bound. The year-end liability rose from $10,313M to $15,148M; a 5% change in the consolidated liability moves revenue by roughly $897M (10-K FY2025, Critical Accounting Estimates).

Contract structure: Lilly has no backlog, no remaining performance obligations, no take-or-pay commitments from customers and no escalators. Payment terms are 30–70 days and product ships shortly after order. Revenue is invoiced at list and reduced by an estimated rebate accrual that settles later; prior-period adjustments have run under 2% of consolidated revenue, which on FY2025 is up to $1,304M either way. Q1 2026 revenue included an undisclosed favourable one-time adjustment to rebate estimates on both Mounjaro and Zepbound, worth about $40 per Zepbound script on the CFO-endorsed arithmetic, or roughly $285M on US Zepbound alone [estimate: (reported − normalized) price × scripts, both from the Q1 2026 call].

Customer of record: three wholesalers — McKesson, Cencora and Cardinal Health — each accounted for between 16% and 24% of consolidated revenue and between 20% and 29% of receivables in 2025, and Lilly does not say which is which.▪ No other customer exceeds 10%. The decision-maker at the point of purchase splits three ways: in reimbursed obesity, four gates (employer, PBM, prescriber, patient copay); in self-pay, one gate (the patient, often after a telehealth consultation); in diabetes, conventional pharma economics with coverage above 90% and the fight over rebate depth.

1.3 The other four franchises, briefly

Established cardiometabolic ($11,713M). This is three unrelated businesses. Trulicity ($4,276M) is a closed installed base declining as patients switch away: Medicare Part D beneficiaries declined 16% to 788,716 in 2024 and dosage units 23.5%, while the injectable GLP-1 basket it sits in grew from 4.0M to 19.8M claims (CMS Part D Spending by Drug, 2020–2024, pulled 2026-07-28) [web]. Lilly's own CEO calls the cannibalisation deliberate: "Tirzepatide has made Trulicity... a lot less used prior to its patent expiry" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). Jardiance ($3,431M) is not a product sale at all but a contractual share of Boehringer Ingelheim's net sales, running only through 31 December 2028 in the most significant markets, and reported growth is flattered: strip the $370M 2025 amendment benefit and the $200M milestone and underlying revenue declined 5.9%.▪ The insulins ($4,006M) are a shrinking, price-reset annuity — Part D beneficiaries for Humalog declined 6.2% a year from 2020 to 2024 while gross price per mL declined 77% in 2024 alone.

Oncology ($9,376M). Seventy percent of it is oral, sold through specialty pharmacy, and 23% is infused biologic under buy-and-bill. Verzenio is 61% of it. The economic unit is a patient-year: US Verzenio runs roughly 21,700–25,000 patient-years at $138,000–$160,000 of net price against $1,000–$4,000 of product cost, a 97–99% product gross margin▪ [estimate: list price less a 25–35% blended gross-to-net; two independent volume angles converge at ~23,000 patient-years]. Two angles produce that count: revenue divided by net price, and a bottom-up build from Lilly's own 2020 sizing of the monarchE-eligible US population (about 20,000 patients meeting the trial's criteria) at a fixed two-year course. Adjuvant Verzenio is an incidence annuity with a hard 24-month duration cap, so once penetration of that fixed pool saturates, revenue growth reverts to incidence growth plus price. Management said so: "overall market penetration has reached a plateau, as reflected in U.S. trends" (Q4 2025 call), and US Verzenio grew 1% in FY2025.

Immunology ($5,247M). Taltz is 68% of it. The disclosed exclusivity is a 2030 US compound patent and 2028 US biologics data protection. Taltz's US net price is $2,324–$2,992 per 80mg unit against a $7,261.51 list, a 59%–68% gross-to-net [estimate: SSR Health 2019 net-to-list anchor, bounded held-flat and eroding, validated against CMS Part D unit and beneficiary shares]. That means Lilly invoices roughly $5.7bn–$7.3bn of gross US Taltz to report $2,333M of net. The two growth assets, Ebglyss ($408M) and Omvoh ($265M), are disclosed only on quarterly slides; Olumiant's ~$1,011M is a residual that reconciles independently against Incyte's disclosed royalty. Two licensor royalties sit in cost of sales and are quantifiable: Roche on Ebglyss at high single digits to high teens ($37M–$69M in FY2025) plus up to $975M of milestones payable, and Incyte on ex-US Olumiant at a realized 18.6%–19.5% ($140M–$152M). Together that is 3.4 to 4.2 points of segment gross margin given away on two of four products.

Neuroscience and other ($2,334M). Kisunla and Emgality are the same modality made the same way at nearly the same cost per gram, and their economics diverge on channel rather than on clinical merit▪: Kisunla is physician-administered and reimbursed under Medicare Part B at ASP-plus through buy-and-bill with no PBM in between, while Emgality is dispensed at retail into a formulary auction with six branded entrants. On the estimates that can be built, Kisunla retains roughly 85–90 cents of every list dollar and Emgality roughly 30–45 cents [estimate: Lilly's published $695.65 and $741.69 WAC prices against booked revenue and CMS Part D gross spend; the Part D leg could not be re-verified — see the source list]. Kisunla's revenue per patient is capped by design because dosing stops when amyloid clears, so lifetime revenue per patient is bounded near $37,500 and every future dollar must come from a new patient start [web, unverified: the vial schedule and the TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 completion percentages behind that figure could not be re-fetched].

A gap that bears on this section: revenue equals patients times refills, and Lilly discloses neither. Management asserts "great persistency overall relative to other chronic conditions" (Q1 2026 call) and publishes no discontinuation curve, cohort retention or refill rate. Every script-to-patient conversion here and in Section 17 assumes twelve scripts per patient-year. Published external work on real-world GLP-1 persistence exists and was not gathered in this run; if two-year persistence is materially below twelve months of refills, the patient counts implied by the script forecasts are wrong in the same direction.

2. Key technologies and technical differentiators

Lilly's technical differentiation is real but narrower than the share numbers imply, and it does not sit where management's framing puts it. Three things are separable: the molecules, the physical plant, and the development organisation.

Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonism (tirzepatide). A once-weekly, fatty-acid-modified 39-amino-acid peptide agonising both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors. The operative pharmacology is central rather than pancreatic: Skovronsky describes "brain receptors for GLP and GIP, amylin and glucagon" regulating "food and food craving" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). The measured performance delta against the only scaled rival is a head-to-head trial: SURMOUNT-5 produced 20.2% weight loss on tirzepatide 15mg against 13.7% on semaglutide 2.4mg at 72 weeks (Lilly press release 2024-12-04, accessed 2026-07-28) [web].

What is not proprietary is the biology. Novo reached 22.7% with CagriSema, a GLP-1 plus amylin combination containing no GIP agonism at all; Amgen reached roughly 20% with MariTide, a GLP-1 agonist and GIP antagonist; Roche and Zealand advanced an amylin analogue to Phase 3 [web]. Three mutually contradictory pharmacologies reach roughly the same weight loss, which is direct evidence that dual agonism is a route to the destination rather than the only route.▪ The moat argument should not rest on the receptor combination.

What is hard is the accumulated clinical library and the physical plant. Lilly has run tirzepatide through heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, adolescent type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular outcomes, MASLD, morbidity and mortality in obesity, type 1 diabetes, and Phase 3b combinations with two of its own immunology biologics. Replicating an indication library of that width takes a decade of trial capacity even with an equally good molecule.

Oral non-peptide GLP-1 agonism (orforglipron, marketed as Foundayo). Licensed from Chugai in October 2018 for a $50.0M acquired IPR&D charge when it was pre-clinical; Chugai receives tiered royalties of mid single digits to low teens on worldwide net sales, booked in cost of sales. Approved in the US in April 2026. The technical claim is manufacturing economics rather than efficacy: roughly a 16-step convergent small-molecule synthesis instead of solid-phase peptide synthesis, estimated 30–50% below peptide-competitor manufacturing cost, no cold chain, and no sterile fill-finish requirement▪ (mewburn.com, themedicinemaker.com, both accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. Skovronsky: "it's just a normal small molecule, so we can make it at scale. It doesn't require refrigeration or biotechnology" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). Ricks names the commercial purpose: in "very populous middle-income countries with large absolute obesity populations like India, like China, Indonesia, Brazil, it's just not going to be possible to reach those people with parenterally manufactured injectables" (J.P. Morgan, 2026-01-13).

The efficacy claim does not survive testing in obesity. Foundayo delivered 12.4% weight loss at the top dose in ATTAIN-1 over 72 weeks. Novo's oral semaglutide 25mg delivered 16.6% in OASIS-4 over 64 weeks and was approved in the US in December 2025, four months earlier [web].▪ Structure Therapeutics' Phase 2b aleniglipron delivered 15.0–15.3% at 44 weeks [web]. Lilly's own ADA deck confines its oral superiority claim to type 2 diabetes, where ACHIEVE-3 compared Foundayo against oral semaglutide 14mg — the diabetes dose, not the 25mg obesity dose — and produced 74% greater relative weight loss (2026 ADA Investor Event, slides 6 and 10). Foundayo's edge in obesity is scale, no food-or-water restriction and a completed cardiovascular safety package, not depth of weight loss.

Next-generation molecules. Retatrutide, a GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist, produced 28.3% mean weight loss at 80 weeks on 12mg in TRIUMPH-1 and 30.3% at 104 weeks in an extension of 532 participants with baseline BMI at or above 35, with 65% of top-dose participants reaching a BMI below 30 and 33% below 25 (2026 ADA deck, slides 18–20). The engineering result that gets less attention is the 4mg dose: 19% weight loss reached with a single titration step and placebo-like adverse-event discontinuation, against five steps over 20 weeks for tirzepatide 15mg. The offset is tolerability at the top dose — 11% discontinuation for adverse events against 5% on placebo, plus a class-atypical dysesthesia signal at 12–13% against 1% (slide 23). These are cross-trial comparisons against products studied in different populations and estimands, so the ranking is indicative. Eloralintide, a selective amylin receptor agonist claiming at least tenfold selectivity for AMY1R over AMY3R, produced 12.4% weight loss at 3mg with no titration and placebo-like tolerability (nausea 13% against 14% on placebo), and 16.4% at the escalating dose with no plateau at 48 weeks (slides 25–26). Amylin is now the most crowded next-generation target in obesity, with Novo, Roche/Zealand and Pfizer/Metsera all holding Phase 2/3 assets, so Lilly's claim is a medicinal-chemistry advantage rather than a target advantage, and it is testable in Phase 3.

The physical platform. This is the technology with the strongest evidence of durability and the least disclosure. Capital expenditure was $7,841M in 2025 against $5,058M in 2024, up to approximately $10bn of take-or-pay contract-manufacturing exposure over terms generally up to eight years, and 13 sites under construction split between an API-and-dry network and a parenteral-and-devices network (JPM 2026 deck, slide 5). Management states $55bn of commitments since 2020. The 10-K states the barrier plainly: "Shifting or adding manufacturing capacity is a very lengthy process requiring significant capital expenditures, process modifications, and regulatory approvals." Aseptic fill-finish capacity is regulator-qualified line by line and product by product and cannot be bought forward.▪ Ricks estimates that "the 2 leading GLP-1 companies have like 80% of the capacity" of the world's parenteral sites (JPM, 2026-01-13), an assertion with no disclosed derivation.

Two facts cut against reading the plant as a pure asset. The take-or-pay obligation and the fixed-cost base convert a demand miss into a margin event, which the 10-K names directly. And the platform is being repositioned rather than only expanded: Foundayo needs oral solid-dose capacity, a different network from the parenteral one, so to the extent the market shifts oral, Lilly's parenteral advantage becomes less relevant to the marginal patient, and it is Lilly that is driving the shift.

Other platforms. Amyloid-targeting antibodies (Kisunla approved in the US, EU and Japan; remternetug in Phase 3) run into a binding constraint in diagnostic and infusion infrastructure Lilly does not own. In targeted oncology, pirtobrutinib is the only approved non-covalent reversible BTK inhibitor, which is a mechanistically distinct position rather than a me-too, and Lilly reports four positive Phase 3 CLL trials including an 80% progression-free-survival risk reduction against bendamustine-rituximab and 76% against ibrutinib in treatment-naive patients (Q1 2026 deck, slide 17). Radioligand therapy from POINT, in vivo base editing from Verve, siRNA and gene therapy are all pre-revenue. Devices are outsourced to unnamed third parties and the 10-K's intellectual-property table lists no device patents, so the KwikPen is a convenience feature rather than a differentiator.

The development organisation. Skovronsky: "we decided about a decade ago that the #1 organizing principle for R&D was to try and be the fastest in every task... We're about 3, 3.5 years faster than the average company" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). The 3.5-year figure is footnoted on Lilly's own slide to a proprietary study by KMR, a WCG company, covering 2022–2024, with no public version; the "24 NME launches from 2015–2025" on the same slide has no such footnote and is Lilly's own launch tally; the 42 active Phase 3 programmes is a separate CFO disclosure on the Q1 2026 call. The observable proxies that do support the speed claim are the breadth of the Phase 3 slate and the Foundayo submission cadence, filed in 40–45 countries in parallel for both obesity and type 2 diabetes, which Skovronsky calls the fastest global parallel path in Lilly's history.

Skovronsky states Lilly invests "more in R&D as a percent of our revenues than anyone else in this industry" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). R&D intensity has declined for three years — 27.3% (FY2023), 24.4% (FY2024), 20.5% (FY2025), 17.7% (Q1 2026) — because revenue outran a rising R&D dollar.▪ AstraZeneca reported FY2025 revenue of $58.7bn with core R&D above $14bn, an intensity above Lilly's. The claim holds in dollars and in history; as a statement of current intensity it does not.

The exclusivity clock is a technology decision, and it is shorter than the patent table. Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid synthetic peptide, which the FDA regulates as a drug under a New Drug Application rather than as a biologic. The 10-K states the rule: government-set Medicare prices apply "beginning at nine years (for medicines approved under a New Drug Application) or thirteen years (for medicines approved under a Biologics License Application) following FDA approval." Mounjaro was approved in May 2022. The same patent table lists tirzepatide US data protection expiring 2027 — the five-year new-chemical-entity term of an NDA, not the twelve-year biologics term — which identifies which clock applies. Orforglipron, a small molecule approved in 2026, restarts the same nine-year clock. Lilly's two largest technology bets both chose the modality with the shorter regulatory economic life, and the 10-K says so: the nine-year timeline "reduces the attractiveness of investment in small molecule innovation."

3. Competitive advantages and moat assessment

3.1 The consolidated position

Lilly earns returns far above any plausible cost of capital and holds a real, multi-layer advantage in the incretin franchise, but the advantage is being converted into volume rather than price, and the price line is declining fast enough to be the central question about durability.▪ Four things are defensible: a US compound patent on tirzepatide to 2036, a European one to 2037 and a Japanese one to 2040; an efficacy edge over the only scaled rival that is demonstrated head-to-head and visible in share; the largest manufacturing base in the industry for this modality; and a direct channel to the patient that does not pass through a pharmacy benefit manager.

Three things cut the other way, and all three are in the disclosed numbers. The efficacy advantage does not show up in price — US realized price declined 10% in FY2025 and 10% again in Q1 2026 excluding the one-time rebate adjustment, consolidated price went from (6)% to (13)%, and management guides a low-to-mid-teens decline for FY2026. An advantage that cannot be monetised in price is a volume advantage. The cost advantage over Novo Nordisk is small: Lilly's Q1 2026 gross margin of 81.9% reported and 82.6% non-GAAP sits one to two points above Novo's adjusted 80.6%, not the ten-point gap a durable scale-cost advantage would produce, and Novo bought three Catalent manufacturing sites for $11.7bn in December 2024 to close the capacity gap.▪ Manufacturing scale is a barrier to a third entrant; against the second it is worth about two points of gross margin. And the franchise consumes capital heavily: free cash flow margin was 13.8% in FY2025 against a 45.6% core operating margin, because capital expenditure ran at 12.0% of revenue and inventory rose from $4.3bn to $13.7bn in three years.▪

Against the three calibration points, this is not Visa/Mastercard network economics or Google search — those earn structural excess returns against well-funded attackers without heavy defensive reinvestment, and their pricing is not set by three wholesalers, three pharmacy benefit managers and a government. Nor is it a no-edge, price-taking commodity: the returns are extraordinary and the share record shows a real product advantage converted into position. It is the middle case, an advantage that earns excess returns today and is defensible for now but open to erosion, and it sits at the strong end of that case, because the erosion vector is price and policy rather than share loss.▪

Business-model analogues. The closest reference class is Gilead Sciences in hepatitis C and HIV: a best-in-class, patent-protected molecule in a category the company effectively created, throwing off enormous cash on a finite clock, whose realized price declined hard once a credible rival and concentrated payers arrived.▪ The shape holds precisely — one molecule, one buyer bloc, spectacular returns, a dated ceiling — and it breaks in two places: obesity penetration is only mid-single-digit percent of the eligible US population where hepatitis C was curative and therefore self-depleting, and Lilly has a four-deep succession pipeline that Gilead did not have. Novo Nordisk is the literal analogue: the same moat construction of molecule intellectual property plus peptide manufacturing scale plus a prescriber franchise, differing only in that Novo is now the one losing share and guiding FY2026 adjusted sales down 4% to 12% at constant currency against Lilly's plus 28% at the midpoint. ASML is the analogue for the capacity leg alone, and it is where the analogy breaks most usefully: peptide fill-finish is not extreme-ultraviolet lithography, it was available for purchase, Novo purchased it, and orforglipron's oral solid-dose form removes the barrier from the next generation of the franchise entirely.

3.3 The financials the moat has to leave behind

Definitions used throughout this section, stated once:

Core operating income = revenue − cost of sales − R&D − marketing/selling/administrative, before acquired IPR&D and before impairment/restructuring. All-in operating income = core operating income − acquired IPR&D − impairment/restructuring. NOPAT = operating income × (1 − reported effective tax rate; 20% substituted for 2017, when the Tax Act charge produced a 103.7% rate). Invested capital = total equity + total debt − cash and equivalents − short-term investments. ROIC = NOPAT ÷ average invested capital. The peer table below uses ending invested capital for every company including Lilly, so the two bases differ and both are shown. Cost of capital: assumed ~7.5%, range 7.0–8.5% — a stated assumption, not a computed weighted average, used only to establish that the spread is very large.

Standalone, ten years: core ROIC sat in a 33–40% band across 2018–2023 and then stepped up to 47.9% in FY2025 (35.1% all-in on ending invested capital, 42.5% on average invested capital)▪. Incremental returns are the sharper measure: every incremental dollar of capital deployed since the tirzepatide ramp began has earned roughly 40% after tax — ROIIC of 43.1% core over 2020–2025 and 44.0% over 2022–2025. The incretin franchise did not create the excess return; it multiplied an already-high one.

The number that cuts against moat quality is cash conversion. Free cash flow margin was 20.1% in 2022 at a 29.0% core operating margin and 13.8% in 2025 at a 45.6% one. Invested capital rose from $23,176M to $60,013M in three years, and Lilly guides "meaningfully higher capital expenditures in the near term." A structural moat of the Visa/Mastercard type does not require this. This one does.

3.4 The four non-incretin franchises

Franchise Assessment Closest analogue
Established cardiometabolic No durable advantage. What it has is a runway with a contract date on it: three years of remaining US Trulicity exclusivity, three years of a royalty on a molecule Lilly does not own, and no exclusivity at all on the third that is insulin. The behaviour is a price-taker's — US Trulicity revenue declined 21% in 2025 and 22% in Q1 2026 with no generic or biosimilar dulaglutide on the market, and Lilly's own low-price insulin versions achieved, in management's words, "minority market shares." One thing is real: patient-level stickiness, which buys duration and not price. This is the third calibration case — returns at or below the cost of capital over any horizon that includes the contractual expiries Merck's Januvia/Janumet by mechanism; Organon by structure; AbbVie's US Humira by magnitude of a payer-driven reset, breaking because Humira's reset needed actual biosimilar entry while Trulicity's did not
Oncology High gross economics and two first-in-class positions, but the advantage is asset-level and time-limited rather than firm-level, and the largest asset is past its inflection. The franchise is sub-scale: $9,376M against Merck's roughly $34.9bn, AstraZeneca's $25,618M and J&J's $25,380M, each computed from that company's own filing. Verzenio is 61% of it, grew 1% in the US in 2025, and has its Medicare price set by HHS from 2028. Middle calibration case, at the weaker end of it AbbVie's oncology book (Imbruvica/Venclexta refreshed by bolt-on M&A) and Bristol-Myers Squibb oncology: a molecule portfolio on a patent clock renewed by R&D and deals, with none of the compounding of a network or benchmark franchise
Immunology Earns high returns today and will for a few more years, but the three tests fail or cannot be run. Pricing power is absent — Lilly names Taltz alongside Zepbound as a driver of the US price decline in Q1 2026. Scale is absent — $5,247M against AbbVie's $30,406M, with Skyrizi alone 3.3x the whole Lilly franchise. Switching costs are weak and the switching decision belongs to the PBM. Taltz is 68% of the segment, declined 3.8% worldwide and 12.6% in the US in Q1 2026, and its US biologics data protection expires 2028. The one thing a competitor cannot copy is that Lilly owns tirzepatide and has run the only Phase 3b programme adding an incretin to an immunology biologic — 27% of patients on tirzepatide plus ixekizumab hit the TOGETHER-PsO co-primary endpoint against under 6% on ixekizumab alone. That is prospective and entirely unrealised in revenue. Middle case, weaker end Amgen's inflammation book (Enbrel, Otezla, Tezspire) and BMS's immunology book. AbbVie's immunology franchise is the counter-analogue: it shows what the same model produces when the player has enough scale to sequence a successor generation before the cliff, and Lilly has not demonstrated that here
Neuroscience and other No durable advantage. Kisunla has the longest protected runway of any Lilly product — US compound patent and biologics data protection both to 2036, on the thirteen-year IRA clock — and US prescription leadership in a class that produced roughly $250M in FY2025, 0.4% of company revenue. It has no pricing power (Part B buy-and-bill, list within about 20% of Leqembi's), no switching costs (the limited-duration course removes the annuity by design), no measurable scale or cost evidence, and a diagnostic gate owned by third parties. Emgality is losing a rebated class to oral gepants and Lilly stopped disclosing it after FY2024's $870.4M. Second calibration case with a qualification: the advantage is a time-limited legal exclusion right rather than an economic moat Biogen on structure (FY2025 revenue $9,891M, five-year CAGR (6.0)%, 6.1% ROIC); Amgen's Aimovig franchise on the class dynamic; Gilead's hepatitis C franchise on the finite-course revenue shape

4. Competitive landscape and market sizing

4.1 Incretins: a duopoly whose sides swapped

Two firms sell every branded incretin analog of consequence. Concentration on the two-company revenue pool is as high as a two-firm market allows, with an implied Herfindahl index above 5,000 on every basis.▪ What changed is which side is bigger.

Basis Lilly Novo Implied HHI
Global incretin revenue, FY2024 41.1% 58.9% 5,159
Global incretin revenue, FY2025 53.5% 46.5% 5,024
Global incretin revenue, Q1 2026 ~62% [estimate] ~38% [estimate] ~5,288
US total prescriptions, Q1 2026 (IQVIA) 60.1% 39.4% 5,165
International gross revenue, Q1 2026 (IQVIA MIDAS) 53.2% 46.8% 5,020

The pool is built from the two producers' own reported revenue rather than from third-party market sizing. Lilly's incretin total (Mounjaro + Zepbound + Trulicity) was $21,720M in FY2024, $40,784M in FY2025 and $13,741M in Q1 2026 (10-K FY2025 Note 2; 10-Q Q1 2026 Note 2). Novo's GLP-1 total (Ozempic + Rybelsus + Victoza + obesity care) was DKK 214,271M and DKK 234,549M, converted at 6.8953 and 6.6149 [web]. The Q1 2026 Lilly share rests on an estimated Novo residual for Rybelsus and Victoza held at the FY2025 run rate, and is sensitive to that estimate; the FY2024-to-FY2025 move of 12.4 percentage points is computed entirely from disclosed figures.

This matters because widely circulated third-party sizings do not reconcile. One 2026 source puts 2025 global GLP-1 sales at approximately $132bn and tirzepatide products at over $62bn [web]; the two producers of essentially every branded incretin analog in the world reported $76.2bn of combined FY2025 revenue. Any penetration or TAM work built off the larger figure overstates the base by roughly 1.7x.▪

US market, bottom-up. Zepbound at ~7.0M prescriptions and $591 realized, Mounjaro at ~9.0M and about $470, Trulicity at ~1.2M — 17.2M Lilly prescriptions at a disclosed 60.1% share gives a total US incretin analogs market of about 28.6M prescriptions in Q1 2026, or 2.2M a week.▪ Lilly's own deck charts put the type 2 diabetes market at ~1,380k and branded obesity at ~880k weekly, summing to 2.26M; the two methods agree within 3%. At a 28-day fill that implies roughly 8.8 million US patients on a branded incretin. Lilly's own June 2025 slide put April 2025 at "8 million" prescriptions against a "170M+ by 2030" addressable count and called that 5% penetration; the 170 million is a prevalence count of people with obesity or overweight-with-comorbidity plus type 2 diabetes, not a demand or payer-covered estimate, and should be treated as a ceiling.

The two sub-markets are growing at completely different rates, and Lilly's share is moving in only one of them.

US sub-market, Q1 2026 Prescription growth YoY Lilly's position
Incretin analogs — obesity +80%+ Zepbound ~64% share, flat for four quarters
Incretin analogs — type 2 diabetes +11% Mounjaro ~51%, up about 9 points over four quarters
Combined +30% 60.1%, down 0.4 points in the quarter

That combination explains the flattening consolidated share line: Lilly is still taking share in the market that has stopped expanding, and holding share in the market that is doubling.▪ The Q1 2026 dip is the first sequential decline in a series that had moved one way for six quarters, and it coincided with Novo's Wegovy pill reaching 207,000 weekly US prescriptions by launch week 15. In dollars a 0.4-point move on a market growing 30% is trivial; as a signal it is the first negative datapoint in the series.

Non-marketed competitors, sized by the only KPI that exists. Eight Phase 3 programmes are running and none can reach market before 2028: Amgen's MariTide (monthly or less-frequent injection, ~20% at 52 weeks in Phase 2); Pfizer's MET-097i and PF-3944 via the Metsera acquisition, completed at $65.60 a share in cash plus a contingent value right of up to $20.65, an enterprise value of approximately $7.0bn, with ten Phase 3 studies to initiate in 2026 (Pfizer completion release, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]; Roche's enicepatide and petrelintide; AstraZeneca's elecoglipron plus a CSPC alliance; Viking's VK2735 in both forms; Structure's aleniglipron; Kailera/Hengrui's ribupatide and oral KAI-7535; and Boehringer/Zealand's survodutide. Amgen's monthly and Pfizer's ultra-long-acting injectables attack dosing frequency, the one dimension on which tirzepatide holds no advantage.

Generic semaglutide is already marketed in India from March 2026 and Canada from January 2026, in markets holding roughly a third of the world's adults living with obesity [web].▪ Lilly's evidence that this expands rather than takes the category is three weeks of Indian data, and its own executive frames it as category expansion rather than switching: Jonsson said generic entry "seems like it's really stimulating the growth in the overall obesity market, and that includes our product," with Mounjaro prescriptions "about 10% higher in recent weeks compared to the period prior," and drew the conclusion that "dual agonist trumps single agonist" (Q1 2026 call). That is a short window in one market against a structural pricing rule — Canadian rules force injectable prices to 35% of brand once three generics are marketed [web, unverified].

4.3 Share counter-evidence, ranked

  1. The oral segment resets the price and convenience frontier, and Lilly entered second. Within one quarter Novo's pill was running at roughly 28% of Zepbound's weekly US prescription volume.▪ Approximately 19,830 weekly Foundayo prescriptions in the week ended 26 June 2026 against approximately 149,000 for oral Wegovy, both flat-to-down sequentially [web, unverified], with Foundayo three months younger.
  2. Generic semaglutide in eight markets in 2026, concentrated in exactly the geographies where Lilly's growth now sits: ex-US Mounjaro was 49% of Q1 2026 franchise growth.
  3. The US obesity share plateau. Zepbound at about 64% for four quarters, with the headline share line dropped from Lilly's Q1 2026 slide 8 — where it had appeared every quarter through Q4 2025 — while the underlying 13-week chart on slide 26 continues.
  4. Eight Phase 3 obesity programmes from Amgen, Pfizer, Roche, AstraZeneca, Viking, Structure, Kailera and Boehringer, none reaching market before 2028.
  5. Government price-setting. Trulicity was selected in January 2026 for prices effective 2028; the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge programme runs only to 31 December 2027, and Part D plans declined to opt in for 2027.
  6. Compounders retreating, which is a tailwind rather than a threat: Hims and Ro exited compounded GLP-1s in early 2026 [web].

5. Value chain and profit pools

Only the retail-pharmacy chains were analysed. The physician-administered Medicare Part B chain through which Kisunla, Cyramza, Erbitux and Tyvyt move, roughly $10.8bn or 17% of FY2025 revenue, was not decomposed, and its price mechanism (average sales price plus a percentage, set on a lagged reported average) and its binding constraint (diagnostic and infusion capacity) are different from the ones described below. The three ex-US pricing regimes that set 33% of revenue — European reference pricing and health-technology assessment, Japan's biennial revisions, and China's NRDL — were examined only for China.

Lilly sits in two structurally different chains for the same molecule, and the split between them moved fast in 2025–26.

Chain A, the reimbursed channel: Lilly to one of three wholesalers, to a retail or mail pharmacy, to the patient, with a pharmacy benefit manager adjudicating the claim, setting the pharmacy's reimbursement and collecting a rebate.

Chain B, LillyDirect self-pay: Lilly to LillyDirect to a third-party dispensing pharmacy to a patient paying cash. No wholesaler, no PBM, no rebate, no chargeback, no formulary. Telehealth partners supply the prescriber [web].

5.1 One dollar of US list-price spend on Zepbound, reimbursed channel

Inputs: a $1,086 monthly wholesale acquisition cost [web]; $4,134M of Q1 2026 US Zepbound revenue on about 7.0 million prescriptions; the CFO-confirmed $550 normalized blended net; 45% self-pay at a $299–$449 published price. Solving for the reimbursed-channel net gives $673, with a $632–$714 range across a $350–$450 self-pay realization [estimate: disclosed blended net per script, disclosed channel mix, solved for the residual].

Layer Named companies Revenue capture per $1.00 of list Gross margin at that layer Operating profit per $1.00 Who sets the price at this interface
Manufacturer Eli Lilly $0.58–0.66 net [est] 83.0% consolidated FY2025; tirzepatide above average $0.24–0.30 [est] Lilly sets list; the PBM sets the rebate that determines net
Wholesaler McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal Health ~$0.98 gross flow-through 2.72% (Cencora US segment, all products); explicitly lower on GLP-1 ~$0.00–0.01 A distribution service fee negotiated as a share of list; near zero on GLP-1
Dispensing pharmacy CVS, Walgreens, independents, mail acquires ~$0.98, reimbursed ~$0.96 [web] about (2)% on the drug ~$(0.01)–0.00 The PBM sets reimbursement unilaterally
PBM CVS Caremark, Express Scripts, Optum Rx fee plus a retained share of the ~$0.38 rebate 3.8–4.6% adjusted operating margin on segment revenue, all products $0.00–0.04, wide [est] The PBM, via formulary placement
Concession leaving the chain plan sponsors, employers, CMS, state Medicaid, 340B entities $0.34–0.42 n/a n/a Statutory (Medicaid's 23.1% minimum, 340B) or negotiated

Layer margins are computed from each participant's own FY2025 filing: Cencora US Healthcare Solutions gross margin 2.72% and operating margin 1.23%; McKesson North American Pharmaceutical segment operating margin 1.09%; Cardinal Health Pharma 1.12%; CVS Health Services adjusted operating margin 3.76%; Optum Rx 4.6%; Evernorth 3.07%.

No intermediary layer captures the missing 34 to 42 cents. The wholesaler earns about one cent of operating profit per dollar across all products and says explicitly that it earns less on GLP-1 — Cardinal Health: "increased GLP-1 sales did not meaningfully contribute to segment profit"; Cencora: US gross margin rose 30 basis points "offset in part by higher sales of GLP-1 products, which have lower gross profit margins." The dispensing pharmacy loses money on the molecule; the pharmacy-acquisition and reimbursement percentages behind that are an industry estimate rather than a disclosure [web]. The PBM's operating margin on its whole book is 3.8–4.6%, and its GLP-1 economics are almost certainly below that because rebate pass-through to plan sponsors is near-total in large contracts. The PBM's retained economics on a GLP-1 script is the one cell in this table with no independent angle: pass-through terms are contractual and undisclosed on both sides. What happens to the residual is that it leaves the commercial chain entirely and accrues to employers, health plans, CMS, state Medicaid agencies and 340B entities as a price reduction.

That is a different structure from a chain where a powerful intermediary extracts the profit pool. The intermediaries here earn a fee on volume at thin margins, and their power is to deny access rather than to capture margin. That is why Lilly's response was a parallel channel rather than a price fight.▪

5.2 The self-pay dollar

Layer Named companies Revenue capture Notes
Manufacturer Eli Lilly $299–$449 sticker less an undisclosed fulfilment fee Lilly sets the price unilaterally
Dispensing pharmacy Gifthealth and other third-party pharmacies undisclosed per-fill fee "Delivery of select Lilly medicines dispensed by third-party pharmacies" (10-K FY2025)
Prescriber Ro, Teladoc, LifeMD, 9amHealth, Form Health, knownwell the patient pays the telehealth platform separately [web]
Wholesaler, PBM none zero Both layers removed

Per script Lilly realizes less in self-pay (about $400 mid-range) than in the reimbursed channel (about $673). The self-pay channel is volume-accretive and access-protective, not price-accretive, costing roughly $273 per script against the reimbursed alternative on this arithmetic.▪ The counterfactual is not real, because most of those prescriptions would not exist at $673 to a cash payer.

5.3 The binding constraint, and where it moved

Supply was the constraint through 2024 and is not now. The FY2024 10-K stated that "at various times during 2024 demand for our incretin medicines exceeded production"; the FY2025 10-K deletes that language entirely and inserts an overbuild risk in its place. The cleanest quantitative marker is the contingent take-or-pay obligation to contract manufacturers, and it also shows a disclosure change that matters:

Filing Disclosed maximum Population covered, in the filing's own words
10-K FY2022 ~$4.5bn "The executed agreements" — expansion for "our incretin products"
10-K FY2023 ~$10bn same incretin framing
10-Q Q3 2024 $11.5bn "primarily related to our incretin medicines"
10-K FY2024 $14bn "primarily related to our incretin medicines, including medicines in development"
10-Q Q1 2025 through 10-K FY2025 $8bn rising to $10bn "Executed agreements related to our medicines in development"
10-Q Q1 2026 not disclosed The paragraph is absent; the surrounding liquidity text is repeated verbatim

The headline declined 29% between the FY2024 and FY2025 10-Ks at the same time capital expenditure rose from $5.1bn to $7.8bn and construction in progress rose from $8,245M to $13,013M. The decline is a population change, not a reduction in obligation: take-or-pay on commercial-stage incretin manufacturing dropped out of the disclosed figure and has not been disclosed since.▪ The last comparable full-population figure is the FY2024 10-K's $14bn, now eighteen months stale.

A residual physical constraint sits downstream rather than upstream. On the Q3 2024 call Lilly attributed the channel-inventory swing to wholesalers and retailers "making their own decisions about which of the 12 different dosage forms they want to stock and at what level... Cold chain capacity is constrained. And there are financial constraints, working capital that they're managing to." The 10-K generalises it: "incretin volume fluctuations due to channel dynamics or demand can have a disproportionate impact on our results of operations in any given period." This is one reason the oral matters structurally: a solid oral dose removes cold chain from the downstream layers entirely.

5.4 Customer-side economics and bargaining power

Lilly's economic customer is not the wholesaler that takes title; it is whoever decides whether the drug is covered. The 10-K states the mechanism: "in the U.S. self-insured employers must generally opt in for coverage of anti-obesity medicines. Payers in various international markets also do not cover anti-obesity medicines for weight loss." Commercial access has been "pretty steady around 50%" of lives through a period of maximum publicity while franchise revenue roughly doubled (Yuffa, Q1 2026 call). At a reimbursed net near $673 per member-month, one covered member costs a plan roughly $8,100 a year. The self-pay channel exists because that arithmetic does not clear for a large share of employers.

At the supplier interface, power is moving toward Lilly: contingent contract-manufacturing obligations declined while capital expenditure rose 54%, and supply now exceeds US demand for tirzepatide. Three qualifications apply. Royalties on the future franchise sit in cost of sales — Chugai on orforglipron at mid single digits to low teens, Roche on Ebglyss at high single digits to high teens plus up to $975M of milestones — so the oral GLP-1 management describes as the next leg of growth is the one product with a permanent third-party claim on its gross margin, while the injectable that produced 56% of FY2025 revenue has none▪. Novo Holdings acquired Catalent for $16.5bn in December 2024 and Novo Nordisk took three fill-finish sites from it; trade press names Catalent among Lilly's GLP-1 fill-finish contractors and Lilly names no contract manufacturer in any filing, so whether Lilly depends on capacity owned by its principal competitor cannot be resolved from disclosure. And the 10-K names dependence on "China-based suppliers for portions of our supply chain, including integral chemical synthesis, reagents, starting materials, and ingredients" without quantifying it, against the BIOSECURE Act and tariffs.

At the customer interface, power is moving away from Lilly at every point. CVS Caremark stopped covering Zepbound as a preferred obesity medicine on some plans in July 2025, which the 10-K concedes "has negatively impacted access." Jardiance is subject to a government-set Medicare price from 2026 at a 66% discount to the 2023 list; Trulicity and Verzenio were selected in January 2026 for 2028. Mounjaro's NRDL inclusion in China cost 25% of ex-US realized price in a single quarter. Both sides of the PBM interface now name the other as a structural threat in their own risk factors: CVS's FY2025 10-K flags that direct-to-consumer sales by manufacturers "may... adversely impact the performance of the Company's Pharmacy & Consumer Wellness and Health Services segments," while Cigna's discloses that Evernorth will make negotiated discounts available upfront at the counter from 2027–2028.

Circular financing is largely absent. Lilly funds supplier capacity (up to ~$10bn of take-or-pay, $200M into Pharmaron, more than $1bn into Indian contract manufacturers [web]) but the supplier is not a customer, so no demand loop is created. There is no vendor financing, no equity stake in a wholesaler, PBM, plan or pharmacy, and no guarantee of customer purchases. The one real loop is patient assistance, which sits inside the $62,135M of US gross-to-net reductions and means some share of reported demand is manufacturer-subsidised; the amount is not separately disclosed. The dependency that does exist runs the other way: Lilly has committed five-to-eight-year fixed capital and take-or-pay obligations against a price that third parties reset annually.

The November 2025 agreements added a new term to that trade. Lilly received a three-year exemption from Section 232 tariffs "provided that we meet U.S. manufacturing investment commitments" (10-K FY2025). The $50bn-plus US build is now partly a regulatory obligation rather than purely a commercial choice.

6. Secular and industry trends

The geography gap flagged at the top of Section 5 applies here too: outside-US revenue was $21,698M in FY2025 and the ex-US realized-price line moved from 0% to (25)% in one year, but only the China mechanism was decomposed. Europe more than doubled from $4,299M (2022) to $11,558M (2025) with no decomposition of how much is Mounjaro launches, how much is Jardiance collaboration revenue, and how much is the one-time collaboration-amendment benefits. Japan has declined in absolute dollars since 2020 while every other region grew, and this run did not explain it.

6.1 Growth attribution against the realized record

Lilly's own MD&A decomposition, ten years:
