Revenue levels for 2016–2018 in this table are as originally reported and include Elanco; Section 13's continuing-operations basis shows $19,974M for 2017 and $21,493M for 2018, and the percentage columns are Lilly's as disclosed in each year's MD&A.

Volume growth has accelerated for four consecutive years and is still accelerating. The price line inverted: a modest and steady drag through 2022, positive in 2023–24, and now the largest negative in the ten-year record.

The claimed secular driver did appear, and appeared larger than management framed it. The claimed driver that did not appear is pricing power. US realized price was +9% in 2023 and +8% in 2024, which the FY2023 10-K attributes to "decreased utilization of savings card programs as access continued to expand" rather than to list-price increases. That was a gross-to-net repair on a small base, it runs once, and it has fully reversed. Volume growth and price decline are now the same variable, because every incremental access channel Lilly is opening prices below the current blended realized price▪:

Channel Net price per 30 days Against the ~$580 Q1 2026 implied US Zepbound realization
US commercial insured undisclosed; the residual implies the highest above
LillyDirect self-pay $299–$449 below
TrumpRx cash ~$350 stepping toward ~$245 over two years [web] below
Medicare Bridge / Medicaid $245 (patient copay $50) [web] well below
China NRDL undisclosed; drove ex-US price (25)% in Q1 2026 well below

The organic bridge. Lilly's acquisitions over this period were pipeline and platform purchases expensed as acquired IPR&D, not revenue-generating businesses, so no acquisition bridge is needed. Divestitures do need one. FY2023 revenue includes $1,450M of net gain on the olanzapine portfolio sale and $579M on Baqsimi, both recognised as revenue. Adjusting FY2023 to $32,095M: 2023 organic growth was +12.5%, not +19.6%, and 2024's was +40.3%, not +32.0%. Anyone chaining the reported series understates the 2024 acceleration by eight points.▪

The peer growth cohort, split by incretin exposure. FY2025 revenue growth in US dollars: Lilly +45.0% and Novo Nordisk +6.4% (+10% constant currency) in the incretin-exposed cohort; a fifteen-name non-incretin large-cap cohort with a median of +4.0% and a mean of +4.1%, running from Sanofi +10.3% and Amgen +10.0% down to Takeda (2.5)% and Pfizer (1.6)% [web]. Lilly's ex-tirzepatide business grew +0.3% in 2025, below the non-incretin cohort median; on the narrower ex-tirzepatide, ex-Trulicity basis it grew +4.6%, at the median. Neither basis supports a claim that Lilly's non-incretin portfolio is outgrowing the industry. The 45% headline is the molecule.▪

Novo is the direct test of whether this is a class effect or a company effect. In 2025 Novo grew +10% at constant currency against Lilly's +45%. In Q1 2026 Novo's adjusted net sales were DKK 70,063M, (4)% year on year, and Novo guides FY2026 adjusted sales to (4)% to (12)% at constant currency while Lilly guides +28% at the midpoint. Two companies in the same class are growing at opposite signs, so this is a company effect.

Market growth against company growth. On the two producers' own reported revenue, class value grew 51.4% in 2025 while Lilly grew 121.7% and Novo's combined GLP-1 book grew 14% in dollars. Lilly captured 82.0% of the class's incremental dollars in 2025 — $20,041M of a $24,455M increase. Lilly is taking share from Novo, not merely growing with the class.

Volume tells a different story and both are true. Novo reports that global branded GLP-1 obesity volume grew 104% in 2025 and that its own global branded obesity volume share was 59.6% [web]. Novo holds a volume majority and a value minority. The reconciling variable is price per unit: Novo's volume sits disproportionately in lower-priced international and Saxenda channels.▪ Anyone quoting "Novo leads obesity share" is quoting volume; anyone quoting "Lilly leads" is quoting value.

Where claimed drivers did not appear.

  • "Multiple growth engines beyond incretins." Ex-tirzepatide revenue was $28,058M in 2022 and $28,672M in 2025, roughly zero growth over three years. This became visible for the first time in Q1 2026, when ex-tirzepatide, ex-Trulicity revenue grew +10.5%.
  • "Neuroscience as the next leg." Kisunla revenue was $124M in Q1 2026 against $22M a year earlier. That is real growth, and it is 0.6% of quarterly revenue.
  • "Orals expand the market for Lilly." Foundayo ran approximately 19,830 weekly US prescriptions in late June 2026 against approximately 149,000 for oral Wegovy, both flat-to-down sequentially [web, unverified], with Foundayo launched three months later. So far orals have expanded the market more for Novo than for Lilly.

6.2 Penetration, and the ceiling

Management's own figures are the best available and are directional: US penetration of the eligible obese population is "only mid-single digits" (Q4 2025 call); globally, Ricks put it at "something like 1% of obesity penetration today" and called the move from 1% to 5% "a big lift" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). Lilly frames the addressable population as "over 1 billion people around the world with obesity and related conditions." That is a prevalence count, not a willing-and-able-to-pay count. The constraint is neither patients nor manufacturing capacity — Lilly resolved the shortage in late 2024 and has committed $7.8bn of 2025 capex plus up to $10bn of take-or-pay — but a payer, and at $245–450 a month a payer who will fund only a fraction of the prevalence pool.

Third-party sizing shows how little anyone knows: IQVIA puts obesity medicines at $66bn of list-price sales value in 2025, forecast to $92bn in 2026 and "between $105 billion and $200 billion" for 2027 and beyond (iqvia.com, accessed 2026-07-28) [web]. The 2027-plus range is a factor of two wide.

6.3 The dated policy calendar

The IRA clock on tirzepatide is the single largest dated risk to the slope, and it is not the 2036 date in the patent table. The FY2025 10-K's patent table shows tirzepatide US data protection expiring 2027, the five-year new-chemical-entity term, rather than the "biologics data protection" label it uses for Trulicity, Taltz, Emgality and Kisunla. On the disclosed rule, that puts tirzepatide on the nine-year clock from the May 2022 Mounjaro approval. Applying the statutory intervals — seven years elapsed at the selection publication date, price applying no earlier than nine years post-approval, publication on 1 February two years ahead of the applicability year — the first qualifying publication is 1 February 2030 for an initial price applicability year of 2032 [estimate: IRA statutory arithmetic applied to the disclosed approval date; CMS's proposed rule for the 2029 cycle onward is not final, so the year is uncertain by about one year in either direction]. The same statutory arithmetic supports 2031 or 2032, and that dispersion is the honest answer.

Whichever year it lands, the economically binding date is roughly four to five years before the 2036 patent, and Lilly is opening Medicare access on 1 July 2026, which builds precisely the Part D gross-spend base that determines selection ranking.▪ The already-realized version of the same mechanism: Jardiance's government price took effect in 2026 at $197 per 30-day supply against a $573 CY2023 list, a 66% discount; comparable first-cycle cuts were Farxiga 68% ($178.50 against $556) and Januvia 79% ($113 against $527), from the CMS selected-drug price table [web]. Trulicity and Verzenio were selected in January 2026 for 2028. Those three products were $13,430M, 20.6% of FY2025 revenue. Lilly's own risk factor states the expectation: "we expect additional products will be selected in future years, which would have the effect of accelerating revenue erosion."

The November 2025 US government agreements committed Lilly to a net $245 per 30-day supply for Medicare and Medicaid, a Medicare Bridge programme starting no later than 1 July 2026 and running through December 2027 with $50 patient copays, state Medicaid opt-in at the same price, and participation in TrumpRx at cash prices starting around $350 [web]. Two details from the Q1 2026 call cut the other way. Part D plans declined to opt in for calendar 2027 — Ricks: "we had understood at the time that there was a commitment to '27 as a contingency, if the Part D plans did not choose to opt in at a certain rate. Of course, we now know they didn't" — so the government extended the Bridge rather than converting it into a standing benefit, and the 2028 arrangement is unresolved. And Lilly lost Medicaid access in certain states in Q1 2026, a high-single-digit drag on Zepbound prescription growth.

Generic semaglutide from 2026 is a slope change for the international business in both directions, and it arrives in exactly the geographies driving Lilly's growth. The December 2025 EU agreement-in-principle to revise pharmaceutical legislation, setting base data protection at eight years and reducing the maximum protection available by one year, is a newly disclosed, dated ex-US erosion affecting future launches rather than the current book.

6.4 Cyclical against secular

Lilly is not macro-cyclical. Its cycle is the patent and launch cycle, and the disclosed record covers a complete one.

Phase Years Revenue Rate
Pre-Cymbalta-cliff level (revenue peaked in 2011 at $24,287M) 2013 $23,113M —
Cliff (Zyprexa, Cymbalta, Evista) 2013 to 2014 $23,113M to $19,616M (15.1)% in one year
Trough and rebuild 2014 to 2021 $19,616M to $28,318M +5.4%/yr
Incretin ramp 2021 to 2025 $28,318M to $65,179M +23.2%/yr

The 2014 trough is the base rate for what a Lilly patent cliff does, and it is directly relevant because the current book is more concentrated than the Zyprexa-era book was: tirzepatide at 56% of FY2025 revenue and 64.8% of Q1 2026 revenue exceeds any single product's share in 2011.

6.5 What the disclosed KPIs would show first if the story were breaking

Ranked by how early each turns and how reliably Lilly discloses it:

  • Share of new prescriptions rather than total. Lilly publishes it quarterly on its market slides, and it turns before total prescriptions because the total lags by the persistence of the installed base.
  • Revenue per prescription. Derivable each quarter as US brand revenue divided by IQVIA prescriptions, this is the number that distinguishes trading price for volume by choice from losing price to competition.
  • The US price line in the MD&A decomposition. The specific signal is a widening gap between the reported figure and the "excluding one-time adjustments" figure management volunteers.
  • Gross-to-net realization from the annual roll-forward. Two consecutive years of falling net realization would confirm the channel-mix explanation.
  • Self-pay share of Zepbound prescriptions, and commercial employer coverage percentage.
  • Persistence and discontinuation, which Lilly discloses in no KPI at all and which is the largest measurement gap in the franchise.
  • Foundayo weekly prescriptions against oral Wegovy.

7. Critical points

1. One molecule is 65% of the company and the concentration is still rising. Tirzepatide went from 1.7% of revenue in 2022 to 56.0% in FY2025 to 64.8% in Q1 2026, and six products were 82% of FY2025 revenue against 75% in FY2024. Non-incretin revenue was $28,058M in 2022 and $28,672M in 2025, compounding at 0.7% a year. Two of the five franchises are in absolute decline.▪ The base case in Section 17 has incretins at 80% of revenue by 2031, because orforglipron is also an incretin. A tirzepatide-class event — a safety signal, a label change, a manufacturing consent decree — hits roughly two-thirds of revenue at once, and the FY2025 10-K adds a sentence absent in FY2024: "Our dependence on, or focus in, one or more key products or product classes exacerbates this risk."

2. Volume is being bought with price, deliberately, and the price line has more than doubled its rate of decline in one year. Consolidated realized price went from +5% (FY2024) to (6)% (FY2025) to (13)% (Q1 2026), against volume of +27%, +50% and +65%. FY2026 guidance embeds a low-to-mid-teens price drag on $82–85bn of revenue, roughly $11–14bn of revenue given up against flat price [estimate: mid-point price drag applied to the revenue guide midpoint]. The mechanism is management's own: "pretty much every time we reduce pricing, we see a pretty large expansion," and "the primary pricing effect in Q1 are actually negotiated outcomes with governments" (Ricks, Q1 2026 call). Every disclosed access channel Lilly is opening in 2026–27 prices below the channel it displaces.

3. The three payer constituencies that bear the risk each declined to fund the product within twelve months. Part D plans did not opt in for calendar 2027, so the government extended the Bridge instead. Commercial employer access has been flat at about 50% of lives. California removed Medicaid obesity coverage for 2026. Meanwhile the access that does arrive is priced at $245 a month against roughly $550–580 of realized US net revenue per Zepbound prescription, a 55% reduction on every prescription that migrates. Access arrives as volume at a lower price, and it converts some of the currently-undiscounted medical-exception and sleep-apnea volume that supports today's realized price.

4. The gross-margin climb has stopped and reversed, and the two margins are now moving in opposite directions. Quarterly gross margin peaked at 84.3% in Q2 2025 and has declined three consecutive quarters to 81.9% in Q1 2026, with FY2026 guided "relatively stable to slightly down... offset by price and new facilities coming online." Non-GAAP performance margin over the same span went from about 43% to 47.2% to 50.0%. The price drag is landing in gross margin while operating leverage on both R&D (+28% against +56% revenue in Q1 2026) and marketing/selling/administrative (+19%) more than offsets it. The ten-year gross-margin climb from 73.1% in 2016 has ended; whether the operating leverage continues is a spending decision rather than a manufacturing constraint.▪

5. The economically binding exclusivity date is roughly 2031–2032, not 2036. Tirzepatide is a 39-amino-acid peptide approved under a New Drug Application, so it sits on the IRA's nine-year clock from the May 2022 approval rather than the thirteen-year biologics clock. Consensus contains no exclusivity event for tirzepatide inside its forecast window at all; consensus revenue rises every year through 2035 on the mean. The only trace of the alternative anywhere in the consensus panel is the FY2031 EPS standard deviation of 25.9% of the mean and a mean below the median, which is a minority of contributors modelling a break the average washes out.

6. Free cash flow converts at less than half of earnings, and the gap is deliberate. FY2025 free cash flow of $8,972M is 43% of net income; after the $3,008M of cash spent on in-process-R&D asset acquisitions — which sits in investing while the charge is added back in operating — it is $5,964M, or 29%.▪ On a three-year-smoothed basis net income per share compounded at 21.4% from 2014–16 to 2023–25 while free cash flow per share compounded at 6.6%. Capital expenditure went from 4.9% of revenue (2016) to 12.0% (2025); inventories went from $5,773M (2023) to $13,744M (2025) with days on hand at 454; and $12.9bn of the balance sheet is prepaid tax on unrecognized intercompany profit, primarily Irish, up from $7.1bn. That last item should reverse as inventory sells, which materially changes any forward cash-conversion assumption.

7. Construction in progress is 35% of gross property and equipment and produces nothing yet. $13,013M at 31 December 2025, up from $8,245M, against gross property and equipment of $37,235M. Bringing it into service adds roughly $650–900M of annual depreciation into cost of sales on top of 2025's $1,314M [estimate: 15–20 year blended life], a 50–70% step-up before any of the remaining programme is spent. Lilly rewrote its own risk factor to add the overbuild case, deleting the FY2024 language about demand exceeding production and inserting "overestimation of demand... may result in supply imbalances." The peer base rate for that mechanism is Pfizer's $6,199M of COVID-19 inventory write-offs in 2023 alone.

8. Business development is running at a size the stated framework was not built for. Across 2017–2025 Lilly spent about $27.7bn of cash on external innovation, and Ricks sizes the 2025 programme himself: 39 transactions, "$4 billion of capital across all those." In the first five months of 2026 Lilly closed Ventyx for $1,058M net, disclosed up to approximately $12 billion payable at closing on pending acquisitions, and announced three vaccine acquisitions "totaling just under $4 billion." Depending on whether that last figure is at-closing or includes milestones, 2026 year-to-date consideration at or near closing is roughly $15–17 billion in under six months, against $27.7 billion across the whole of 2017–2025. The framework Skovronsky describes — run the NPV but rank it low, screen on unmet need, science and team, and expect the portfolio to work "in bulk" — is coherent for buying many small early-stage options and has not been restated now that a single cheque (Centessa, about $6.3bn at closing) exceeds the entire prior-year programme.

9. Disclosure narrowed in the year realized price turned negative. The FY2025 10-K withdrew the instrument-level notes table (43 instruments replaced by nine maturity buckets), the operating-lease maturity schedule, the credit-facility assurance language, the fixed/floating swap sentence, and product-level revenue lines for the insulins, most of oncology, Olumiant and Emgality; the following 10-Q dropped the take-or-pay commitment paragraph. Each was found by hand in this run rather than by a systematic diff, so the complete list is unknowable from the work as done. The practical consequence is that the debt stack, the fixed/floating mix and the lease ladder in Section 12 are reconstructions from the FY2024 filing rolled forward.

10. Nothing in the incentive plan charges management for capital. No return on invested capital, no free cash flow, no capital-efficiency measure appears in the annual bonus, the long-term plan, or the three measures Lilly names as most important. Acquired IPR&D — roughly $11.4bn net of tax since 2021 — is added back to the bonus EPS metric by design and sits outside the "performance margin" metric Lilly now guides on. A $7.8bn capital programme appears in no metric at all. Each individual exclusion has a coherent argument; the aggregate is a management team measured on the revenue of seven growth products, EPS before its own investment spending, an undisclosed pipeline score, and the share price.

8. Management claim pressure tests

"Manufacturing scale is the moat." Management repeats it every quarter: "Since 2020, we've committed over $55 billion, the largest manufacturing build-out in company history." Capacity is what a rival buys. Novo acquired three former Catalent sites for $11.7bn in December 2024 and ran capital expenditure at 19.5% of sales in FY2025 against Lilly's 12.0%. If the capacity lead produced a durable cost advantage it would appear as a gross-margin gap; the actual gap in the latest comparable quarter is 1–2 points (Lilly 82.6% non-GAAP against Novo 80.6% adjusted), and both are declining for the same reason. The manufacturing leg is worth roughly two points of gross margin. What the $55bn buys is the ability to serve demand at price points that expand the market, and a barrier to a third entrant.

"Price cuts are volume-accretive, so the price drag is a strategy rather than a problem." The elasticity is demonstrated in launch cohorts, not in the installed base. The 95% ex-US volume growth against a 25% price decline comes from newly-launched countries where penetration started near zero, which is a first-fill effect rather than a re-order elasticity.▪ In the US, where the base is mature, volume grew 49% against a 7% reported price decline and the growth is explicitly attributed to new patient starts. Meanwhile the non-GAAP gross margin has begun to move in the direction the elasticity argument says it should not: 83.6% (Q3 2025), 83.2% (Q4 2025), 82.6% (Q1 2026); the reported series runs 82.9%, 82.5%, 81.9% over the same three quarters. Asked directly for the margin sensitivity to price on the Q1 2026 call, Ricks answered with elasticity and gave no number.

"The price declines are policy one-offs; underlying price is stable." The per-channel claim survives the arithmetic and the consolidated claim does not. Covered-channel net revenue per US Zepbound script was roughly $630 in Q1 2025 and roughly $673 in Q1 2026 (range $632–714), so the blended decline is channel mix rather than per-channel erosion. But the CFO's statement that prices "have been relatively stable quarter-on-quarter" applies only after carving out the most-favoured-nation agreement and the NRDL listing, and each carved-out item is a separate counterparty exercising the buying power the market structure gives it. Three consecutive years of high-single to mid-teens realized price decline compounds to roughly a 20% lower price per unit by end-2026 against FY2024 [estimate: compounding the disclosed consolidated rates], on a molecule with a patent to 2036.

"Most of the Q1 2026 price decline is geographic mix." Weighting Lilly's own regional price lines from its Q1 2026 slide 7 (US (7)%, Europe +5%, Japan +2%, rest of world (4)%; China marked not meaningful, with the slide's footnote saying China price is lower on NRDL inclusion) by prior-period regional revenue gives a revenue-weighted regional price change of about (4)% against the reported consolidated (13)%. The reconstruction is validated because it reproduces Q1 2025 revenue at $12,707M against the actual $12,729M and reproduces the reported 52% consolidated constant-currency growth exactly. The same test on FY2025 gives (6.7)% weighted against (6)% reported, so there was no gap a year ago; the divergence appeared exactly as ex-US Mounjaro passed US Mounjaro. Lilly does not publish its decomposition methodology, so this is an inference from two of its own disclosures on one slide.

"LillyDirect and self-pay route around the PBMs and are a structural advantage." It is also an unrebated, price-elastic channel with no formulary lock-in, no contracted volume, monthly cancellation and a competitor one click away, and Lilly declines to size it in dollars anywhere. Per script Lilly realizes less in self-pay (about $400 mid-range) than in the reimbursed channel (about $673). Lilly has already cut its own direct prices twice within roughly twelve months. Novo priced high-dose Wegovy at $399 a month cash-pay in April 2026, undercutting most Zepbound doses [web]. The 10-K names the risk in its own words: "risks related to the level and pace of patient participation in cash-pay markets, which may be influenced by pricing, economic conditions, and competitive offerings."

"Penetration of the obese population is the growth driver." The reimbursed channel did not grow. Commercial access has been steady around 50% of lives for at least a year and California removed Medicaid coverage for 2026. Franchise growth came from self-pay, which went from roughly zero to 45% of Zepbound prescriptions in six quarters, and from ex-US launches, which supplied 49% of Q1 2026 franchise growth. Penetration of the eligible population is a demand ceiling; it becomes a driver only if somebody funds it.

"Net price erosion is a sector condition every large pharmaceutical company is absorbing." The peers' own FY2025 filings do not show it. Amgen reported product sales +10% on volume +13% and net selling price (3)%, and guides Repatha to a mid-single-digit price decline for 2026. Merck reported the opposite sign on its two largest franchises: Keytruda US growth "reflects higher demand and net pricing," and diabetes growth was "largely attributable to higher net pricing of Januvia." Pfizer reported "favorable net price in the U.S." on oncology biosimilars. Lilly's consolidated realized price decline is roughly 2x Amgen's in FY2025 and roughly 4x it at the Q1 2026 run rate.▪ The mechanism behind the gap is not a formulary exclusion or a biosimilar; it is the November 2025 agreements, the LillyDirect price reductions and the China NRDL listing, each of which Lilly negotiated. That also means it is a choice with an observable reversal path, unlike a patent cliff.

"Tirzepatide's exclusivity runs to 2036." The 10-K's own patent table lists US data protection expiring 2027 — the new-chemical-entity term — which identifies tirzepatide as an NDA product on the nine-year IRA clock. The already-selected products, Jardiance, Trulicity and Verzenio, were 20.6% of FY2025 revenue, and Jardiance's government price is a 66% discount to its 2023 list. Applying a discount of that order to Medicare volume on two-thirds of the revenue base is a different order of event from a patent expiry in 2036.

"Lilly is taking share in obesity." Lilly's Q1 2026 statement was that obesity prescriptions grew over 80% and "Zepbound prescriptions grew at even faster rate" — true year over year, and silent on the sequential picture. Zepbound's 13-week rolling US share of the branded obesity market has been approximately 64%, 62%, 64%, 64% across the last four quarters. Lilly's actual share gains came from type 2 diabetes, where Mounjaro went from 42% to about 51% over the same period.▪ The headline obesity share line was dropped from the Q1 2026 slide 8 for the first time since the metric was introduced, in the quarter the competitor's oral product launched.

"Lilly out-invests everyone in R&D as a percentage of revenue." R&D intensity has declined for three years: 27.3% (2023), 24.4% (2024), 20.5% (2025), 17.7% (Q1 2026) — because revenue outran a rising R&D dollar. Including acquired IPR&D the series is 38.4%, 31.7%, 24.9%. The peak in the modern record was 24–25% during the 2014–2016 patent-cliff trough, not now. AstraZeneca's FY2025 core R&D above $14bn on $58.7bn of revenue is a higher intensity than Lilly's.

"Verzenio's differentiation case held the CDK4/6 class." Measured in class dollars, Verzenio grew 7.8% to $5,723M in FY2025 while Novartis's Kisqali grew 58% to $4,783M and Pfizer's Ibrance declined 5.6% to $4,122M. Verzenio's dollar share of the class went from 41.8% to 39.1% in one year while the class grew 15.2%. Kisqali sold $1,516M in Q1 2026 against Verzenio's $1,302M, the first quarter in which Verzenio was not the largest CDK4/6 inhibitor.▪

"Taltz's +18% US growth in 2024 showed the brand still had runway." Lilly's own FY2024 MD&A attributes it to "higher realized prices due to changes in estimates for rebates and discounts, as well as increased demand" — an accrual revision first, demand second. Note 2 of the FY2025 10-K puts portfolio-wide adjustments to prior-period rebate estimates at 3% of US revenue in 2024 against under 1% in both 2023 and 2025. The trajectory around it runs +12% (2022), +6% (2023), roughly +8% clean (2025), (12.6)% (Q1 2026).

"Kisunla is the leader in amyloid-targeting therapy." Lilly's claim is a US prescription statement and is accurate on its own terms: "Kisunla recently became the U.S. market leader in the amyloid targeting therapy space with more than 50% share of total prescriptions" (Q4 2025 call). On dollars Leqembi is larger — $168M globally in Q1 2026 against Kisunla's $124M [web]. Eisai's competitive response attacks the economics rather than the label: Leqembi IQLIK, a weekly at-home subcutaneous autoinjector approved for both initiation and maintenance, is priced at a wholesale acquisition cost of $385 per autoinjector [web]. Kisunla's own headline differentiator, a limited-duration course, mechanically removes the annuity: a completed patient stops paying, and Biogen is explicitly building a business catching patients transitioning off Kisunla onto Leqembi maintenance [web].

"Management does not underwrite deals to a financial return hurdle." Skovronsky's actual formulation is narrower: "Most of my peers actually start with like a commercial forecast and an NPV and we do that. Of course, we have to do that. But that's actually pretty low in the priority list" — because forecast sales and actual sales five years later show "no correlation" (Bernstein, 2026-05-28). Lilly runs the NPV and ranks it low, screening on unmet need, quality of science and quality of team, and expecting the portfolio to work "in bulk." A keyword sweep for "hurdle", "IRR", "return on invested capital", "ROIC", "cost of capital" and "NPV" across all 55 archived transcripts returns only clinical and market-access "hurdles", that Bernstein answer, and one R&D-productivity slide. A real discipline is visible in the record: no acquisition above $1.1bn since Loxo in 2019, and an explicit refusal of large commercial-stage deals, through a period when the balance sheet could have funded one and peers were doing $40–70bn transactions.

"Performance margin is a cleaner measure." Lilly introduced non-GAAP performance margin — gross margin less R&D and marketing/selling/administrative, over revenue — as the named metric on the Q1 2025 call, and it is now the guided metric. It had already been guided one quarter earlier without the name: on the Q4 2024 call, "our expected ratio of gross margin less OpEx divided by revenue." By construction it excludes acquired IPR&D, about 4.5 points of FY2025 revenue, and no reconciliation to the prior non-GAAP operating margin has been published. The reported metric and the paid-on metric now exclude the same item, in the same window.

The five inflections

  • 2011–2014: the patent cliff, and the decision not to buy the way out. Revenue declined 19.2% and net income 45.0%. Lilly did not do a rescue acquisition, did not cut the dividend and did not cut R&D — R&D rose from 20.7% of revenue (2011) to 24.7% (2016) because the numerator was held while the denominator collapsed. Derica Rice described the choice: "we chose not to do large M&A as a way of financially bridging our way through that... we would take the hit of the loss of revenue while maintaining our investment in R&D" (December 2016 guidance call). The five-year window in which R&D ran at 24–25% of a shrinking base is the direct source of the current franchise. The decisions themselves are inferred from a revenue and margin series, because no 10-K before FY2016 and no transcript before Q3 2019 was available to this run, so there is no contemporaneous management commentary from the episode this base rate rests on.
  • Nov 2016 to Mar 2019: solanezumab fails and Lilly is rebuilt around it. Inside 27 months Lilly changed CEO, took a $1,670M restructuring charge, shrank headcount by 2,305, exited animal health, retired 12% of its shares and bought its largest pipeline asset in a decade. Gross margin improved 540 basis points and pretax margin 770. Cost discipline at Lilly arrives after a research failure rather than after a revenue decline: three years of falling revenue produced no restructuring; one failed Phase 3 produced a $1.67bn charge within twelve months.▪
  • May 2022 to Nov 2023: tirzepatide launches into capacity built ahead of it. Capital expenditure ran 4.6% of revenue in 2021 and rose every year to 12.0% in 2025. Ricks explains why the commitment has to precede the demand: new capacity "can take 2.5 to 4 years... a big part of the delivery schedule for that is actually the regulatory process itself" (Q3 2024 call). Given a windfall, Lilly builds physical capacity first and returns cash second — cumulative 2021–2025: capex $19,510M, dividends $20,756M, buybacks $10,108M.
  • 30 Oct 2024: the channel breaks the narrative for the first time. Q3 2024 revenue missed consensus by roughly $0.6bn on a wholesaler inventory decrease worth "mid-single digits as a percentage of aggregate US sales." Two durable decisions followed on the same call: Lilly turned on consumer demand generation for the first time ("we launched this drug almost a year ago and have done no advertising"), and management introduced the profitability metric that became guided performance margin. The response to a channel Lilly does not control was to build one it does.
  • July 2025 to 2026: the binding constraint flips from supply to reimbursed price. The realized-price contribution to US revenue growth swung from +11% in Q3 2024 to (10)% underlying in Q1 2026, roughly 20 points across five quarters. Zepbound self-pay went from about 20% of US prescriptions to about 45%, and from over 35% of new prescriptions to 55%. Lilly priced into the volume rather than defending price, and the pre-built capacity from the prior inflection is what makes the concession survivable.▪ The pattern is consistent: insulin list price down 70% with a $35 cap (2023), LillyDirect (Jan 2024), self-pay vials at over 50% off list (Aug 2024), Zepbound direct price to $299 (Dec 2025), the government agreement (Nov 2025), Employer Connect (Q1 2026). Every one bypasses the PBM formulary.

Episodes the current narrative omits or reframes

The COVID antibody windfall ($871M, $2,240M and $2,020M across 2020–22, 7.9% of 2021 revenue, plus a $339.7M inventory impairment) is not mentioned on either of the last two earnings calls, while the "prolonged growth since 2015" framing runs straight through it. The 2023 divestiture gains booked as revenue are adjusted for in-quarter by management but the headline FY2023 growth rate of 19.6% is never restated, and roughly 7.1 points of it is a one-time asset sale. The 2021 pricing frame was wrong by 3x: "mid-single-digit annual net price declines as the overall trend for the coming years" against FY2026 guidance of a low-to-mid-teens drag. And the growth drivers named in December 2016 — Trulicity, Taltz, Basaglar, Cyramza, Jardiance, Lartruvo, baricitinib, abemaciclib, galcanezumab — do not include tirzepatide, which did not enter the late-phase pipeline until 2018. The company that delivered a 45% revenue increase in 2025 did so on a molecule that was not in its own five-year plan when the plan was written.

10. Management, incentives and capital allocation

10.1 Who runs the company

Thirteen executive officers are listed in the FY2025 10-K, and nine of the thirteen have fifteen or more years of Lilly service. David Ricks has been Chair, President and CEO since 2017 with 29 years at the company; Daniel Skovronsky has run all of R&D since 2018, having joined in 2010 through an acquisition; Lucas Montarce became CFO in September 2024 after 24 years inside, including as CFO of Elanco. Acquisitions have supplied two of the three most senior operators — Skovronsky through Avid Radiopharmaceuticals, and Jake Van Naarden, who runs Oncology plus corporate business development, through Loxo.

Seven of the thirteen took new or expanded roles during 2025. Lilly split its commercial organisation into therapeutic-area presidencies, moved Patrik Jonsson from Cardiometabolic/USA to International and Ilya Yuffa the other way, and gave Van Naarden corporate business development on top of Oncology. Deal sourcing now sits with a profit-and-loss owner rather than with the CFO.

The finance seat has turned over four times in eight years — Rice, Smiley, Ashkenazi, interim Brooks, Montarce — with three of those changes inside the 43 months from February 2021 to September 2024, exactly the window in which the incretin franchise went from launch to $36,508M. Both departures produced forfeitures. Smiley's 2020 bonus was reduced to zero, his 2018–2020 shareholder value award was reduced, and every other outstanding equity award granted in 2019 and 2020 was cancelled under the Compensation Recovery Policy; his 2021 summary-compensation total was $244,681, of which $230,831 was salary. Ashkenazi forfeited her 2024 bonus, performance award, shareholder value award and relative value award on resigning for Alphabet. The clawback has been used, not merely published. Only one of the three transitions since 2021 was adverse; one was a poach and one was internal succession.

10.2 What management is paid for

Incentive pay is 94% of the CEO's target compensation and, on average, 88% of the other named executives'. Salary is the only fixed element and there are no time-vested restricted units in the annual grants.

Element Weight What is disclosed 2025 outcome
Annual bonus — product revenue on seven named products 33.3% Key-product revenue $43,658.2M, FX-adjusted to $43,311.4M. Target not disclosed Above target, multiple not disclosed
Annual bonus — EPS 33.3% Target $24.01; result, on the bonus basis, $27.06 Above target, multiple not disclosed
Annual bonus — pipeline progression 33.3% Scored by the Science and Technology Committee. Objectives not disclosed 230%
Blended bonus 218% of target, against a 250% cap
Shareholder Value Award, 50% of long-term incentive Three-year absolute share price against a cost-of-capital hurdle. 2025 grant: $787.73 starting price, 9.48% cost of capital less a 0.78% dividend yield, maximum-payout price $1,316.01 Payout 0–200%
Relative Value Award, 50% Three-year total shareholder return against a fixed fifteen-name peer group, maximum at 30 percentage points of outperformance Payout 0–200%

The seven-product basket is 67.0% of revenue and excludes the declining, price-controlled third of the business — Trulicity, Jardiance, the insulins. Erosion there produces no bonus outcome in either direction.▪ Two of the three bonus metrics have undisclosed targets; Lilly's stated reason is competitive harm.

What is in no incentive plan: no return on invested capital, no return on equity, no free cash flow, no cash conversion, no capital-efficiency measure, no gross or operating margin. The three measures Lilly names as most important are adjusted non-GAAP EPS, total shareholder return and revenue.

The payout record. Of nineteen long-term payout events across three vehicles from 2018 through February 2026, seventeen paid at the cap. The two exceptions were both the Performance Award, a two-year EPS-growth vehicle whose target was set to sell-side consensus for peer EPS growth, and that vehicle was discontinued after 31 December 2024. The Relative Value Award's realized outperformance has exceeded its 30-point maximum threshold by between 5.6x and 9.5x in every cycle. Annual bonus multiples ran 134% (2017) to 225% (2024) and 218% (2025); the pipeline metric — the one with no disclosed objective — has scored at or near the top of the three components in every year the split is published, and it hit the newly raised 250% ceiling in the first year at its raised weight.

Every cap in the structure was raised in the same window: the bonus cap from 200% to 250% for FY2024, and both long-term caps from 175% to 200% for the 2023–2025 grant. At the old bonus cap, the FY2024 and FY2025 payouts would both have been truncated, worth roughly $1.17M to Ricks across the two years [estimate: bonus target × (actual% − 200%)]. In the same year a new General Industry benchmarking peer group appeared — 3M, Abbott, Adobe, AMD, Apple, Applied Materials, Broadcom, Cisco, Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive, Danaher, Honeywell, IBM, Intel, McDonald's, Micron, Nike, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Salesforce, Tesla, Thermo Fisher — alongside the unchanged pharma group. Ricks' target total direct compensation rose 16.7% on a flat salary, from $24.0M to $28.0M; actual summary-compensation total rose 25.5% to $36,698,337, and the CEO pay ratio went from 168:1 in 2023 to 293:1 in 2025.

The in-flight awards are the current evidence on whether the design discriminates. At 31 December 2025 the 2024 shareholder value and relative value awards both stood at their 200% cap, while the 2025 awards stood at 105% and 139%. That 105% is the lowest in-flight mark in the disclosed record; a year into its cycle the 2024 award stood at 129% and has since reached its cap, so an in-flight award below cap is not unprecedented. The 2025 grant's $787.73 starting price already embeds the 2022–2024 run, so the cost-of-capital hurdle is binding on it in a way it has not been before.

Acquired IPR&D and the bonus EPS metric. Lilly publishes three FY2025 EPS figures inside one document: GAAP $22.95, non-GAAP $24.21, and adjusted non-GAAP for the annual bonus $27.06. The bridge from the second to the third is dominated by adding back acquired IPR&D at $3.08 a share. The disclosed EPS bonus target was $24.01, so the add-back alone accounts for the entire distance between the target and the result. FY2023 is the cleanest illustration: reported EPS declined 15.9% and published non-GAAP EPS declined 20.4%, while bonus-basis EPS rose 6.9% and the bonus paid 181% of target. Roughly $11.4bn of acquired IPR&D net of tax since 2021 sits outside the metric. Lilly's stated reason is that the adjustment guidelines exist to remove "incentives to refrain from acquiring new technologies," and the target was set on a zero-IPR&D basis, so the comparison is internally consistent. The consequence is that no metric charges for the capital.

Ownership. Ricks holds 815,535 shares, 412x his salary against a 12x requirement, worth roughly $700M against $36.7M of 2025 pay. He has not sold a Lilly share on the open market since 3 February 2016, across a move from roughly $77 to $1,045, and has bought twice with his own cash into drawdowns — 4,615 shares at $108.38 in October 2019 and 1,632 at $644.77 on 12 August 2025, five days after the ATTAIN-1 session. Every other disposition on his Form 4 record is tax withholding on vesting or a charitable gift. Hedging and pledging are prohibited, net shares must be held a further year after vesting, and no listed individual has pledged shares. Non-employee directors hold almost nothing outright because the annual grant is credited to a deferred stock account; the lead independent director owns zero shares outright and 16,772 deferred units.

Governance context. Combined Chair and CEO since 2017 with a lead independent director. A classified board and 80% supermajority provisions remain in the articles; management has proposed eliminating both twice — in 2024 targeting 2025 and again in 2026 targeting 2027 — and the amendment threshold is itself 80% of outstanding shares, so the prior attempt did not clear the bar. Lilly Endowment Inc. holds 92,190,516 shares, 9.8%, with sole voting and dispositive power, and is expressly carved out of the "Related Person" definition. PNC holds 5.4%, of which 50 million shares are held as directed trustee of the Compensation Trust. Say-on-pay support has been above 94% in each of the last five years and over 96% in 2025. Ernst & Young has been auditor continuously since 1940.

Candor. Negative trial results appear in prepared remarks rather than being extracted in Q&A: pegilodecakin, CYPRESS 1 and 2, the ACTIV-3 hospitalised-patient result, mevidalen, zagotenemab, tanezumab, solanezumab A4 and the OGA inhibitor were each surfaced by management first. Unhelpful numbers get quantified rather than gestured at — the Q3 2024 destock at "mid-single digits as a percentage of aggregate use sales," and the Q1 2026 rebate revision at "excluding this impact, U.S. price will have declined 10%" against a reported 7%. Ricks owned the FY2024 miss in the first person: "There's turbulence. I'll own that." Against that, the largest negative surprise of 2025 was framed as a success: the ATTAIN-1 readout was described in prepared remarks as "positive" and "encouraging" while an analyst on the same call called it "what is widely viewed as disappointing orforglipron data," and management restated the strengths rather than engaging the head-to-head comparison the question posed.

Uses as a share of twelve-year operating cash flow: capex 35%, business development 44%, dividends 46%, buybacks 27%. That sums to 152%, and the excess was debt-financed: net debt rose $31,085M. Lilly generated $52,085M of free cash flow and spent $93,271M on business development, dividends and buybacks combined, so roughly one dollar in three of that spending over twelve years came from borrowing rather than from operations.▪ Free cash flow converted 71% of reported net income across the period, and 37% in the 2023–2025 sub-period.

The composition of business development inverted: acquisitions dominated the early years (Novartis Animal Health $5,283M in 2015, Loxo $6,918M in 2019 — excluding those two, the remaining ten years averaged $606M a year), while purchases of in-process R&D stepped up from $641M in 2020 to $3,944M in 2023 and have run around $3bn since. Because acquired IPR&D is expensed rather than capitalised, this spend never enters invested capital and never becomes an intangible that can be impaired. Goodwill was $5,898M at the end of 2025 against $34.9bn of twelve-year business-development cash. The usual failure signal for a serial acquirer is structurally unavailable for the majority of recent spend.

2023 is the year the framework was tested. Operating cash flow declined to $4,240M on a large cash tax payment while capex rose to $3,448M, IPR&D purchases to $3,944M and dividends to $4,069M. Uses totalled $13.3bn against $4.2bn of operating cash flow; the gap was bridged with $3,959M of new long-term debt, $4,691M of net new short-term borrowings and $1,604M of product-rights sale proceeds. Nothing in the payout, the capex plan or the business-development programme was cut. The buyback was the only line that shrank.

Buybacks follow available cash rather than the price. Within a year, Lilly landed within ±8% of the year's average close in ten of twelve years and beat it by 13.0% in 2022 and 29.9% in 2023. Across years, the correlation between annual buyback dollars and the year's average price is +0.36 while the correlation with the year-on-year price change is (0.11), so spend tracks the price level rather than the direction. The decisive evidence is a specific deferral rather than a correlation: Lilly entered 2023 with $3.25bn of authorised, unused repurchase capacity, spent $750M of it at its own transaction price of $325.65, rolled $2.50bn into 2024 and spent it at $832.67 — including $1.98bn in October and November 2024 at an average of $830.70. The same authorised dollars, deferred by one year, retired 4.67 million fewer shares for identical cash. Authorisation was not the constraint; the ranking of uses was. Management's own description — repurchases "with excess capital" — matches the behaviour exactly, which is why the separate claim of being "opportunistic" does not survive the record.

The largest share retirement of the period is not in the buyback line at all: the March 2019 Elanco exchange offer retired 65 million Lilly shares, 6.1% of the count, at a recorded value of $8,027.5M. Combined with the $4,400M cash buyback, 2019 retired 102.6 million shares for $12,427M. Nothing since has come close. Buyback as a share of year-end market capitalisation declined from 3.58% (2019) to 0.42% (2025), and total shareholder yield went from 3.9% in 2014 to 0.98% in 2025.

The dividend is a formula, not an earnings-linked policy. Eight consecutive increases of 14.7% to 15.4% while diluted EPS growth ranged from (24)% to +184%. Payout declined from 79% of EPS in 2016 to 27% in 2025 and the yield from 2.84% to 0.56%. Management describes increases as "in line with earnings growth over time." The precedent that matters is the opposite tail: declared dividends per share were $1.96 in 2012, $1.96 in 2013 and $1.97 in 2014 through the last patent cliff, then 2% increases for three years. The board has frozen the dividend before.

Capex is the largest and least-tested allocation decision. Cash capex ran 6.0x depreciation in 2025, and the segment note's "expenditures for long-lived assets" measure is a further 10–11% higher ($8,672M against $7,841M) in each of the three disclosed years, so anyone sizing the build-out off the cash flow statement understates it by about a tenth. Treating depreciation as the maintenance floor puts maintenance near $1.3bn and growth near $6.5bn, so roughly 83% of 2025 capex is expansion [estimate: depreciation-as-maintenance proxy; a fairer band is 75–85% growth because the asset base is young]. Management states over $55bn committed since 2020 against $20,899M of actual 2020–2025 cash capex, so roughly $34bn is still to be spent, and the $55bn has no counterpart in any filing line. There is no disclosed return test at the programme level, and Lilly's disclosure does not permit one. Three indirect measures exist: revenue to net property and equipment was flat at 2.64x in 2023 and 2025 because the denominator grew as fast as revenue, but on in-service assets only it improved from 5.09x to 5.59x; the physical output target was met and exceeded (1.6x incretin doses in H1 2025 against H1 2024, and better than the 1.8x goal for H2); and the 10-K states the downside plainly.

Q1 2026 against the FY2025 run rate. Operating cash flow $5,333M against $1,666M a year earlier; capex $2,326M (+54%); free cash flow $3,007M against $156M; dividends +15.0% on the rule; buybacks $2,356M, the largest quarter in the twelve-quarter window and 129% above the FY2025 run rate. If that pace holds, 2026 buybacks are about $9.4bn, more than double 2025 and the largest in Lilly's history in dollars, though still under 0.9% of market capitalisation. Q1 is seasonally Lilly's weakest cash quarter — Q1 2025 operating cash flow was 10% of the full year — so the annualised figure understates rather than overstates. Financing turned net-negative at the long end: no long-term issuance against $6,461M in Q1 2025, $750M repaid, and $1,775M of net new commercial paper.

11. M&A, divestitures and deal track record

Lilly's deal structure is disciplined and its deal strike rate is poor.▪

The structural discipline is verifiable. Every transaction in the fifteen-year ledger was paid in cash; Lilly has never issued stock for a target. It has never attempted a mega-merger — the largest deal in the period is Loxo at an $8.0bn headline, about 12% of one year of current revenue, against the $63bn Allergan and $74bn Celgene deals its peers did in the same window. It records almost no goodwill because it structures most deals as asset acquisitions and expenses acquired in-process R&D immediately, so a failure shows up as a charge at signing rather than an impairment three years later. Goodwill was $5,898M at 31 December 2025 against $65,179M of revenue, and no goodwill impairment was recorded in 2023, 2024 or 2025. In the animal-health exit, roughly $6.3bn of purchased assets became $4.2bn of cash at the September 2018 Elanco IPO plus an exchange offer management described as "equivalent to an additional $8 billion share repurchase," with a $3.7bn book gain.

The strike rate is the problem. Six transactions between 2018 and 2024 bought clinical assets at Phase 2 or Phase 3 for a combined $8.8bn, and none has produced an approved product▪:

Deal Charge or price Phase at deal Status now
ARMO BioSciences (Jun 2018) $1,475.8M IPR&D Phase III Pegilodecakin missed overall survival in Q4 2019; "we do not plan to initiate any new trials"
Prevail (Jan 2021) $903.8M consideration Clinical gene therapy PR001 intangible impaired Q3 2022
DICE Therapeutics (Aug 2023) $1,915.5M IPR&D Phase 2 DC-806 discontinued in 2024 "in favor of another molecule in development"
Versanis (Aug 2023) $604.1M IPR&D Phase 2 Obesity-plus-type-2-diabetes Phase 2 halted Sep 2025 for "strategic business reasons" [web]
POINT Biopharma (Dec 2023) $1,338.5M consideration Phase 3 PNT2002 abandoned after SPLASH missed on overall survival [web]
Morphic (Aug 2024) $2,548.5M IPR&D Phase 2 MORF-057 still Phase 2 two years on

And the largest deal earned its return from the asset Lilly said was worth the least. Of Loxo's $4,670.0M of acquired IPR&D, $4,600M was allocated to selpercatinib, which the CFO called "the most substantial single-value component in the transaction." Retevmo has never appeared in the Key Products list and its revenue is not disclosed anywhere; the last disclosed figure is $253.6M for FY2023. LOXO-305, which the same CFO described as "early in development," became Jaypirca: $148M in Q4 2025 and $165M in Q1 2026, up 79% year over year, and now a Key Product. Meanwhile the $980.0M of Vitrakvi contract intangibles from the same deal were impaired in 2024 and $128.0M of Loxo Phase I intangibles in 2021.

The best returns came from small licensing-style asset deals. Chugai's OWL833 cost a $50.0M acquired IPR&D charge in October 2018 when it was pre-clinical; it is orforglipron, approved as Foundayo, and the single biggest reason 2026 guidance was raised. Dermira cost $849.3M net and produced Ebglyss, which grew 141% to $145M in Q1 2026. Mablink's MBK-103 cost $256.6M in December 2023 and is almost certainly sofetabart mipitecan, now in Phase 3 with Breakthrough Therapy designation [estimate: identity inferred from matching target, modality and indication between the FY2023 asset-acquisition table and the FY2025 pipeline table].

This is not a value-destroyer: no impairment trail, no stock issued, no overpaid transformational merger, and one well-timed exit. Nor is it a compounding acquirer on the Danaher or Roper model, where each deal demonstrably raises returns on the whole. It is a research organisation buying call options on other people's molecules, with an option-buying record that so far looks average for the industry and a 2026 position size that is not.

Significant asset acquisitions, expensed at close

These are the deals Lilly does most often. The compound has no alternative future use, so the entire cost is written off to acquired IPR&D on the acquisition date. There is no goodwill, no capitalised intangible, and therefore no subsequent impairment to observe. The write-off is the accounting, so outcome must be judged from the pipeline table.

Synergies, terms and the 2026 step-change

There is no synergy record to track. Lilly has never announced a cost- or revenue-synergy target for any transaction in this ledger, because none is a scale merger. The Loxo call is the only place a financial payback commitment appears, framed as margin and accretion: the deal would "put modest downward pressure on margins in the near term," the "goal is still to achieve 2020 operating income as a percent of sales of 31%," and the acquisition had "the potential to be accretive on a cash basis by 2022." Lilly has not reported against any of the three since, and the operating-margin marker is untestable from an income statement with no operating-income subtotal.

Contingent value rights are the standard risk-sharing structure on gene- and cell-therapy targets: Prevail ($4.00/share, about $160M aggregate, fair-valued at $65.9M, decaying about 8.3 cents a month after 31 December 2024 to expiry on 1 December 2028), Akouos ($3.00/share, about $122M, fair value $66.9M, expiring December 2028), Verve ($3.00/share, about $300M, fair value $177M) and Centessa (up to $9.00/share of a $47.00 total) [web]. Lilly does not disclose whether any has paid out or how the liabilities were released. The only regulator-forced divestiture in the record is Sentinel; no terminated transaction is disclosed in the FY2016–FY2025 10-Ks.

Mar 2026 (closed 4 Mar) Ventyx Biosciences $1,178M total, $1,058M net cash $14.00/sh, all cash (10-Q Note 4)
31 Mar 2026 (closed 24 Jun) Centessa Pharmaceuticals ~$6.3bn at closing, up to $7.8bn $38.00/sh cash + up to $9.00/sh CVR; 40.5% premium to the 30-day VWAP [web]

The Q1 2026 10-Q states: "As part of our business development activities in 2026, we have entered into acquisition agreements, subject to closing conditions. Potential amounts payable at closing for these pending acquisitions would be up to approximately $12 billion." Ventyx at $1,058M closed, plus that $12bn, plus roughly $4bn of vaccine deals is about $17 billion at or near closing in under six months — 61% of the $27.7 billion Lilly spent on external innovation across the whole of 2017–2025. If the vaccine figure includes milestones rather than being at-closing, as every other 2026 headline does, the true at-closing total is nearer $15 billion. Both are multiples of the 2025 base.

The disclosure is hard to add up by construction: the $12 billion is one unquantified-by-deal sentence in a 10-Q liquidity discussion; the vaccine deals appear only as an analyst's aggregate in a conference transcript; and management's own framing — Skovronsky's "we do more deals than anyone else, but we don't necessarily spend more money" — describes the 2025 programme while the 2026 one is running. Whether the pending consideration will be expensed or capitalised is not stated, and because Lilly does not exclude acquired IPR&D from non-GAAP EPS the answer moves 2026 reported and non-GAAP EPS by roughly $10–13 a share at the extreme, against non-GAAP guidance of $35.50–$37.00.

12. Capitalization and balance sheet

Total debt grew from $16,239M at the end of 2022 to $42,503M at the end of 2025 and $43,370M at 31 March 2026 — a 162% increase against a 227% increase in EBITDA, so gross leverage declined from 1.88x to 1.50x and to about 1.27x on a trailing-twelve-month basis through Q1 2026.▪ Interest coverage improved to 29.7x in FY2025 from 14.5x in FY2023. Moody's affirmed Aa3 and moved the outlook to positive on 12 December 2025, naming debt/EBITDA sustained below 1.75x as its upgrade trigger and above 2.75x as its downgrade risk [web]. S&P rates the senior unsecured debt A+ with a stable outlook [web, unverified — the S&P page returned an error on re-fetch]. Lilly's own filings disclose no credit ratings at all.

The FY2025 10-K discloses maturity buckets rather than instruments. The instrument-by-instrument table that FY2021 through FY2024 contained (43 notes) was replaced by nine buckets with stated-rate ranges. The stack below is reconstructed by taking the FY2024 instrument list, adding the February and August 2025 issuances and removing the 2025 maturities.

The reconstruction validates: every bucket with a gap to the filed figure contains non-USD notes and every bucket without one (2027, 2029) is all-USD, so the $765M residual is foreign-exchange revaluation of about $6.1bn of euro, Swiss franc, yen and sterling notes between the two year-end rates. The 2028 bucket includes $750M of floating-rate notes paying SOFR plus 0.530%.

Weighted-average cost of debt: principal-weighted stated coupon of 4.12% across the 53-instrument stack at 12/31/2025, with the floating leg marked at SOFR 3.65% plus 0.530%. Adjusting weights to 12/31/2025 exchange rates lowers it to roughly 4.10%, because the appreciating non-USD notes are the low-coupon ones. Implied full-run-rate annual interest: approximately $1,750M.

The stack splits by issue date: $11,463M was issued at or before 2021 at a 2.15% weighted coupon (27%), and $30,614M in 2023–2025 at 4.86% (73%). Non-USD notes are $6,098M, 14% of the stack, at a 1.28% weighted coupon, and they are designated as net investment hedges so translation moves offset in other comprehensive income rather than in earnings.

Reported interest expense is net of capitalized interest and understates the run-rate cost. Note 11 gives interest expense on borrowings of $895M (2025), $781M (2024) and $486M (2023), and cash payments for interest of $633M, $578M and $404M — both explicitly "net of capitalized interest." Two independent methods bracket the capitalized amount at $440M–$645M in 2025: a month-weighted reconstruction of the ladder gives $645M as a ceiling, and average construction in progress of $10,629M at the 4.12% stack coupon gives $438M as a floor [estimate: two methods, both stated]. The $1,750M implied by the stated coupons is a run-rate on the year-end stack, while $895M is the expense of a year in which $8.9bn of debt was added part-way through, so part of the gap is timing rather than capitalization. The unwind is already visible: Q1 2026 interest expense of $332M against $244M a year earlier is +36% on a debt balance up 2%, and annualises to $1,328M.

The maturity wall is not a risk. $12,342M matures 2026–2030 at a 3.83% weighted coupon, 29% of the stack; $30.2bn matures 2031 or later, including $14.1bn beyond 2050. Refinancing the five-year wall at 5.0% adds $145M of annual interest, and at 5.3% adds $182M — 0.5% to 0.6% of FY2025 EBITDA. Long-term debt with a carrying amount of $42,503M had a Level 2 fair value of $39,799M at 12/31/2025 and $38,233M against $41,595M at 3/31/2026, an 8.1% discount implying a market yield roughly 0.6–0.7 points above the average coupon.

Covenants, security, liquidity. The FY2025 10-K discloses no financial covenants on any instrument and no security or guarantees; the notes are obligations of Eli Lilly and Company, the same entity that owns the operating subsidiaries, and non-controlling interests are described as not material. Undrawn committed facilities totalled $10.1bn at both 12/31/2025 and 3/31/2026 — a $4.0bn facility to December 2029 and a $6.0bn 364-day facility expiring August 2026 — of which $10.0bn backstops commercial paper. That 364-day facility rolls within a month of this run date. Commercial paper went from $4,338M (12/31/2024) to zero (12/31/2025) to $1,775M (3/31/2026). Cash was $5,282M at 3/31/2026, below one quarter of operating cash flow, having declined $1,986M in the quarter. The FY2025 10-K dropped the sentence, present in every filing since FY2016, stating that "there are no conditions that are probable of occurring under which the lines may be withdrawn," and the Q1 2026 10-Q does not restore it.

Leases and pension are immaterial. Total operating lease liability $1,362M, 3.2% of total debt, with an 8-year weighted-average term at a 4.7% discount rate; finance leases are not material. Both retirement plans are overfunded — pension funded status +$558M on a $14,262M obligation, retiree health +$1,501M on $1,274M — with employer contributions of $133M in 2025 against benefit payments funded from $17.6bn of plan assets. The expected 7.9% return on plan assets against a 5.5% discount rate produces a net periodic credit.

Dilution runs the other way. Issued shares declined 14.6% over ten years, from 1,106.1M at 12/31/2015 to 944.8M at 12/31/2025, with nearly two-thirds of that in 2019, when the Elanco exchange and that year's cash buyback together retired 102.6 million shares. Excluding that event the decline is 10.7% over seven years, about 1.6% a year. Gross issuance under employee plans is 0.12%–0.19% of shares a year, an order of magnitude below what the stock-compensation dollar suggests, because grant-date fair value per share is enormous — $844.85 for restricted units, $1,154.90 for relative value awards and $1,056.09 for shareholder value awards in 2025. Stock-based compensation of $626M was 0.96% of FY2025 revenue, the lowest in the ten-year record, and the dollar figure was flat while revenue grew 45%.

Structural balance-sheet risks, ranked

  1. Tax assets and the open transfer-pricing examination — $22.9bn, 20.3% of assets. Prepaid expenses of $14,315M include $12,900M of prepaid taxes at 12/31/2025, up from $7,100M, "largely reflect[ing] taxes paid on intercompany profit not yet recognized, primarily related to Ireland." Deferred tax assets add $9,959M, rising to $11,350M at 3/31/2026. Cash income tax payments increased $4.3bn in 2025, driven by a $4.2bn increase in Ireland. The US examination of tax years 2019–2021 is ongoing and Lilly is pursuing Mutual Agreement Procedure relief for 2016–2018 on intercompany transaction pricing. These are cash payments already made that reverse into the income statement as the intercompany profit is recognised; an adverse examination outcome converts an asset into an expense.
  2. Interest expense understated by capitalization, and the unwind has started. Full convergence toward the $1,750M implied by stated coupons would take roughly $855M off pre-tax income against a FY2025 base of $25,731M, or 3.3%, which is material to EPS modelling and immaterial to credit. Depreciation steps up at the same moment for the same reason.
  3. The sales rebate and discount accrual — $17,382M, 49% of current liabilities. EY named it a Critical Audit Matter, noting the estimate is "challenging because of the subjectivity of certain assumptions" and that "historical rebate information may not be predictive." Three figures circulate and all reconcile on their own basis: the $17,382M balance-sheet line for consolidated rebates and discounts excluding returns; the $15,148M year-end roll-forward of the most significant US programmes; and the roughly $17,940M implied by the "approximately $897 million" 5% sensitivity, which adds the return liability held elsewhere. About 87% of the balance is US, down from 90%. Anyone quoting one as "the" rebate liability is quoting a subset.
  4. Take-or-pay manufacturing commitments — up to $10bn over terms generally up to eight years, on the narrowed development-stage population, with the commercial-incretin figure undisclosed since the FY2024 10-K's $14bn.
  5. Cash uses already exceed operating cash flow. In Q1 2026, uses of $9,161M exceeded $5,333M of operating cash flow; the gap was funded with $1,775M of new commercial paper and a $1,986M cash drawdown. With capex guided meaningfully higher, dividends near $6.2bn and the buyback running at a $9bn annualised pace, either the buyback slows or gross debt keeps increasing. That is a capital-allocation choice rather than distress, and it is the mechanism by which the debt stack grows from here.
  6. The 364-day facility renewal. $6.0bn of the $10.0bn commercial-paper backstop expires August 2026. It has been renewed and upsized each year; the concern is that it is annual, and the FY2025 10-K removed the language about no conditions probable of permitting withdrawal.
  7. Floating-rate and currency exposure, both small but no longer verifiable. Explicitly floating debt is $750M, 1.8% of the stack, plus commercial paper. On top sits an undisclosed swap book: every 10-K from FY2021 through FY2024 stated that Lilly "converted approximately 5 percent of our long-term fixed-rate notes to floating rates through the use of interest rate swaps," about $1.5bn at the FY2024 balance. The FY2025 10-K drops that sentence and the accompanying "all of our total long-term debt is at a fixed rate," replacing them with "we may enter into derivative contracts to achieve an acceptable balance between fixed- and floating-rate debt." The mix cannot be computed from the current filing.
  8. Thin book equity. $26,535M, 23.6% of assets, with debt to equity at 1.60x and tangible equity of $14,116M after goodwill and intangibles. This is an artefact of retiring shares against retained earnings for decades rather than a solvency signal, but book-value screens will misread it.

There have been no episodes of balance-sheet stress in the ten-year record: no covenant breach, no forced equity issuance, no dividend cut, no rating downgrade. The peak was FY2023 at 2.94x gross leverage, the only year above Moody's stated downgrade threshold, caused by a $6.2bn commercial-paper build against an EBITDA base held down by $3,800M of acquired IPR&D.

Bloomberg publishes consensus for revenue, gross margin, EBIT, EBITDA, net income, EPS, capex, free cash flow and dividends per share; it publishes no consensus for operating cash flow, share repurchases, return on equity, return on invested capital or net debt, which is why those lines stop at FY2025. Capex is a single gross line — Lilly discloses no government incentives or disposal proceeds netted into it — but the segment note's accrual-basis "expenditures for long-lived assets" measure runs 10–11% higher ($8,672M in 2025, $5,561M in 2024, $3,830M in 2023). Return on equity is not a useful quality metric here because equity is structurally small: a $3,013M employee-benefit-trust contra-equity account and two decades of buybacks reduced equity to a $2,607M trough in 2019.

13.3 What actually drove value

Growth. Revenue compounded 13.3% a year over 2016–2025 as reported, or 15.3% rebasing 2016 to human-pharmaceutical revenue only. That splits cleanly into 9.4% a year pre-incretin (2016–2021) and 23.2% a year since. Essentially all of the ten-year growth is organic: Lilly spent roughly $12.4bn of cash on business acquisitions and $16.0bn on in-process-R&D asset acquisitions across 2016–2025, but the acquired entities were pre-revenue pipeline companies. The one deal that later produced disclosed revenue is Loxo, which sits inside other oncology.

Margin. Operating margin including acquired IPR&D went from 15.4% in 2016 to 40.4% in 2025, and the decomposition is not what the narrative implies:

Driver 2016 (% of revenue) 2025 Contribution to margin (pp)
Gross margin 73.1 83.0 +9.9
Marketing, selling and administrative 30.8 17.0 +13.7
Research and development 25.0 20.5 +4.6
Impairment, restructuring, other 1.8 0.7 +1.1
Acquired in-process R&D 0.1 4.5 (4.3)
Total 15.4 40.4 +25.0

Operating leverage came predominantly from selling costs rather than from gross margin. Marketing, selling and administrative grew 70% in dollars while revenue grew 207%; R&D grew 151% in dollars, so R&D intensity declined only 4.6 points.▪ The single largest offset is acquired IPR&D, which went from a rounding error to 4.5% of revenue.

Year by year: 2017's collapse to 10.0% is a $1,332M impairment and restructuring charge plus $1,113M of acquired IPR&D, with a 103.7% effective tax rate from the Tax Act transition charge producing a net loss on positive pre-tax income. 2021's gross margin dropped 3.5 points to 74.2% because COVID-19 antibodies were lower-margin. 2023's operating margin declined to 18.9% purely on a $3,800M acquired-IPR&D charge; ex-IPR&D it rose to 30.1%. 2025's gross margin rose 1.7 points on favourable product mix and improved cost of production, partly offset by lower realized prices.

Realized incremental operating margin — change in operating income over change in revenue — was 52% cumulatively over 2016–2025 including acquired IPR&D, and 65% in 2025. That is a high incremental margin and it is accelerating, which is what a fixed commercial infrastructure absorbing a volume surge looks like.

Returns. Return on invested capital on the reported-tax definition was (0.4)% in 2017, high-20s through 2019–2022, 17.8% in the 2023 charge year, then 27.7% and 39.7%. On the ex-IPR&D definition it has been 28–44% every year since 2018. Rolling three-year returns on incremental invested capital tell the reinvestment story: (62.7)% in 2019 and (0.2)% in 2023, the two windows dominated by step-ups in invested capital that had not yet produced operating profit, then 22.3% (2024) and 39.4% (2025). Invested capital rose from $18,347M (2016) to $61,770M (2025), a 237% increase, while net operating profit after tax rose 697%.

Cash conversion has broken down and the cause is identifiable. Operating cash flow was 177% of net income in 2016 and 81% in 2025; free cash flow was 139% and 43%. Three things do it. Capex rose from $1,037M (4.9% of revenue) to $7,841M (12.0%), taking capex to depreciation and amortization from 0.69x to 3.93x. Inventories rose from $5,773M (2023) to $13,744M (2025), a $7,971M build, with days inventory outstanding from 298 to 454 while days sales outstanding barely moved from 97 to 99, so receivables grow with revenue and inventory does not. And prepaid taxes rose from $7.1bn to $12.9bn and are the bulk of the $6,609M prepaid-expenses outflow in the 2025 operating cash flow; adjusting for that build alone puts underlying FY2025 operating cash flow near $22.6bn against a reported $16,813M. Partly offsetting, the rebate liability rose $5,843M, so rebate accruals are financing part of the working-capital build.

A second definitional issue matters for anyone building a cash series. Acquired IPR&D is expensed in the income statement, but the cash for asset acquisitions leaves through investing ("Purchases of in-process research and development" — $3,944M in 2023, $3,346M in 2024, $3,008M in 2025) while the non-cash charge is added back in operating. Standard free cash flow therefore ignores $16.0bn of cash spent over the decade on what the profit-and-loss statement calls an expense. Correcting for it gives FY2023 free cash flow of negative $3,152M and FY2024 of $414M against the headline $792M and $3,760M.

The inflections these metrics reveal, in order of importance: realized price turning from a tailwind to the largest drag in the ten-year record while volume accelerated; the ex-US price line moving from exactly zero to (25)% in a single year on one identifiable event; the US share gain flattening at about 60%; and self-pay going from nothing to nearly half of the largest product's US volume in six quarters.

14. Expectations: internal, external and base rates

Consensus and management agree closely on FY2026 and diverge progressively after it. The headline disagreement is that consensus expands operating margin about nine points between 2026 and 2031 while management has published no multi-year target of any kind since 13 December 2022, and the base rates say no pharmaceutical company has ever expanded operating margin from above 40%.▪

One measurement question sits underneath the whole section and is unresolved: whether Bloomberg's consensus EBIT is struck before or after acquired IPR&D. If after, FY2026 consensus operating margin of 44.5% is +4.1 points against Lilly's FY2025 GAAP margin; if the comparison is made against the ex-IPR&D basis of 44.8%, it is (0.3) points. The sign of the headline margin comparison depends on that answer, which one check against a broker model or the estimate footnote would settle.

Volume "industry-leading volume growth" implied +43% to +45% for FY2026, +37% to +39% for Q2–Q4 [derived: consensus growth less the guided price effect] The quarterly panel requires volume to decelerate by roughly 27 points inside nine months, which no analyst has articulated on any call in the archive, while Medicare access opens on 1 July and consumer advertising for Foundayo starts in Q3 —

Ricks called long-term operating margin "the X factor," dependent on how much R&D Lilly chooses to fund Pharma at ≥30% margin and ≥$20bn revenue: median (8.6) points over five years, 7.1% ended higher, recorded maximum +10.6 points from a 30.9% start. The $33.63 figure sits below the GAAP figure, which means the thin adjusted panel mixes definitions —
