Exclusivity 10-K: "we expect additional products will be selected in future years, which would have the effect of accelerating revenue erosion" No exclusivity event for tirzepatide anywhere in the panel. Revenue rises every year through 2035 on the mean, reaching $153,116M; the slowest year is 2034 at +0.6% Management's own filing says the thing consensus does not model. The only trace of the alternative is FY2031 EPS dispersion of 25.9% of the mean, with the mean below the median Lilly's own 2011–2014 cliff: revenue (19.2)% cumulative, operating margin 28.3% to 13.6% to 8.3%, ROIC 27.6% to 0.7%, a decade to recover

The guidance record. Nine initial full-year revenue guides in nine years; eight finished above the top of the initial range, and the exception (2019) is contaminated by the Elanco disposal. The size of the beat stepped up with the incretin franchise: 2017–2022 beats averaged +3.6% against the initial midpoint, and 2023–2025 averaged +10.4%. The interesting failure is the closing guide rather than the opening one. FY2024 landed at $45,043M against a $45.4–46.0bn range set eleven weeks before year-end, and Lilly pre-announced it at the J.P. Morgan conference. FY2025 ran the other way: opened at $58–61bn, held at Q1, raised to $60–62bn at Q2, raised to $63.0–63.5bn at Q3, and landed at $65,179M — $1,679M above the top of a range set with one quarter left to forecast, and $4,179M above the top of the opening range. FY2026 has started the same way. Lilly's incretin volume forecast error is large in both directions, roughly $4bn on a $60bn base; 2024 registered as a credibility event because that year the sign was negative.

On EPS the record splits in two, and both versions are true. On the reported basis, Lilly missed its own opening non-GAAP EPS guide twice in a decade, in 2022 by 7.4% and in 2023 by 22.9%. On the basis the guide is constructed — excluding acquired IPR&D the company had not yet committed to — Lilly beat its opening EPS guide every year since 2017, by 17% to 33% in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025. The reported-basis misses are what the share price traded on; the ex-IPR&D beats are what the operating business did.

What management stopped saying. The number of guided line items declined from eleven in 2022 to four in 2026. Gross margin, R&D and marketing/selling/administrative guidance disappeared with the 2024 guide, replaced by a single composite ratio; reported GAAP EPS guidance was dropped entirely for 2026, footnoted with a non-reconcilability argument that applied equally in 2023, 2024 and 2025; and other income guidance went at the same time. The performance-margin definition itself changed between the 2025 and 2026 guides — the asset-impairment and restructuring deduction was removed — which is worth 0.74 points on FY2025 actuals, so chaining the guided series across the change overstates 2026 margin expansion by about 0.7 points.

The 2015–2020 framework was explicit and numeric and every element was hit: a minimum 5% average annual revenue growth (delivered 7.3%), operating expense at or below 49% of revenue (delivered just over 48%), and 31% operating margin by 2020 (achieved). The December 2021 Investment Community Meeting set the next one: top-tier volume-driven growth through at least 2030, mid-single-digit annual net price declines, gross margin around 80%, and operating margin expanding to the mid-to-upper 30s with SG&A as the primary lever. Three of the four were beaten. The price commitment broke by roughly 3x.▪ It was last reaffirmed on 13 December 2022 and there has been no December guidance call, and no numeric multi-year target of any kind, since.

The near-term print. Q2 2026 consensus EPS is $6.03 against $8.55 in Q1 on 4.0% higher modelled revenue, which implies about $2,570M of charges in the quarter [estimate: Q1 non-GAAP EPS scaled by the consensus sequential revenue change, differenced against consensus Q2 EPS, times diluted shares]. A second, independent angle confirms the size: FY2026 consensus operating income was cut $2,163M between 3 and 24 July 2026 while FY2026 consensus revenue was unchanged and FY2027 and FY2028 estimates did not move. That is the business-development charge being loaded into the current year and nothing else. Lilly's non-GAAP EPS does not exclude acquired IPR&D; Lilly's guidance excludes charges from deals not yet closed. FY2026 consensus EPS declined from $36.47 to $33.63 between 26 June and 28 July 2026, a 7.8% cut, while FY2026 consensus revenue rose 0.3% and FY2027 consensus EPS rose 0.8%. A demand or price revision would compress FY2027 alongside FY2026 and would show up in revenue. Neither happened.

Where Lilly sits in the pharma expectation cohort. On the same Bloomberg pull and field set, Lilly's expected FY2025–FY2029 revenue CAGR of 17.6% is 2.2x the next-fastest large-cap (AbbVie at 8.0%) against a cohort median of 5.6%, and its EPS CAGR of 25.8% is followed by AbbVie at 17.8% and then a gap to AstraZeneca at 12.0%. Pfizer is modelled at (3.5)% and Bristol-Myers at (5.6)%. The row worth dwelling on is Novo Nordisk: the only other company selling incretins at scale is expected to grow revenue 2.0% a year in local currency through 2029 with a flat operating margin. Consensus therefore assigns Lilly 92.6% of the incremental revenue of the three named incretin players over four years.▪ That assumption is invisible in either company's own panel and appears only when the two are placed side by side.

What the dispersion says. The high-to-low spread on consensus revenue widens monotonically: 10% (2026), 20%, 27%, 33%, 38% (2030). By 2030 the difference between the high and low estimate is larger than Lilly's entire 2025 revenue base. Nothing about the near-term print is in dispute; everything about the shape of the curve is. FY2031 is where the panel breaks: the mean EPS of $66.05 sits below the median of $68.99 with a standard deviation of 25.9% against 8.4% a year earlier, and the analyst count declines from 28 at FY2027 to 16 at FY2031. A mean below the median means the tail is on the downside, and it comes from a minority of contributors rather than a general reset.

Where the reference class breaks. Two arguments against the outside view are strong. The class contains no category creation of this type: every prior pharmaceutical franchise competed for an existing, diagnosed, treated patient pool, while obesity in 2026 is a population-scale, largely untreated chronic indication, and Lilly's own 2024 and 2025 organic growth of +32.0% and +44.7% from a $34bn and $45bn base is already outside the entire 37-year record of the class. That is direct evidence the reference class under-predicts here, and it means the revenue base rate deserves the largest discount. Second, the oral shift changes the cost and capacity structure in a way no company in the class has tested. Two arguments are weak: "Lilly has a deeper pipeline" is unfalsifiable given that the 10-K states R&D cannot be reported by project, phase or therapeutic area; and "scale gives operating leverage" runs against the class record at this margin level, where the compressing mechanism is price and mix rather than fixed-cost absorption. The margin and returns base rates therefore deserve the smallest discount, because the mechanisms that compress them are already visible in Lilly's own FY2025 and Q1 2026 disclosures.

15. Market pricing and valuation history

This section is descriptive. It records what earnings did, what the market paid for them, what was expected and what moved the stock. It contains no valuation judgment: no cheap or expensive, no fair value, no price target, no buy or sell view. Where a source expresses such a view it is reported as that source's, with attribution.

"Perfect-foresight forward P/E" divides the fiscal-year-end price by the next year's actual non-GAAP EPS and therefore uses hindsight; "consensus forward P/E" is the contemporaneous Bloomberg forward multiple at the last month-end of the fiscal year, which is what the market was actually paying at the time. Multiples in both columns are written to the nearest turn.

Four footnotes change how rows should be interpreted. FY2017's GAAP EPS is negative because of a $1.91bn provisional charge under the 2017 Tax Act, producing the only annual loss in the period; the trailing GAAP multiple is marked not meaningful. FY2019's GAAP EPS of $8.89 exceeds non-GAAP EPS because the ~$3.7bn Elanco split-off gain ran through GAAP net income. FY2023's 92x trailing non-GAAP multiple overstates the multiple on operating earnings, because Lilly does not exclude acquired IPR&D from non-GAAP EPS while most peers do: adding it back at the disclosed dollar amounts, treated as fully non-deductible, gives non-GAAP EPS ex-IPR&D of $10.54 (2023), $16.63 (2024) and $27.45 (2025), which puts the year-end multiples at 55x, 46x and 39x [estimate: disclosed acquired IPR&D ÷ diluted shares, added back untaxed]. The FY2025 result cross-checks against Lilly's own bonus-plan adjusted non-GAAP EPS of $27.06, a $0.39 difference. So the headline compression from 92x at end-2023 to 44x at end-2025 is about 55x to 39x on a like-for-like operating base, which is real but roughly half as large as the headline. And FY2019 and FY2023 EV/EBITDA are both flattered on the denominator by divestiture gains recognised in revenue.

By era, from FY2014 to FY2020 the consensus forward multiple ranged 15x to 23x with a median near 20x, so the stock compounded without the multiple expanding. From FY2021 to FY2023 it went 33x, 42x, 47x, peaking at 55.8x in the monthly series in early 2024. From FY2024 to June 2026 it declined to 30x at the last month-end observation, with the 28 July 2026 snapshot at 34.8x. The 12.5-year median of the monthly forward-multiple series is 22.2x, minimum 15.4x, maximum 55.8x.

Ten of the eleven completed years with a return produced a positive price return; the single negative year, 2016, contains the 23 November 2016 solanezumab failure. Ten-year total return from the FY2015 close to the FY2025 close is +1,414% cumulative, 31.2% a year, and over the full price series from 2 January 2014 the total return is +2,940%, also 31.2% a year.

Two of the twelve years have a fiscal-year average close above the fiscal-year-end close: 2016 ($76.38 against $73.55) and 2024 ($810.87 against $772.00). The 2024 case is the informative one. The stock peaked at $960.02 on 30 August 2024 and finished the year 19.6% below that peak, so the +32.4% price return measures from a low start rather than from strength through the year.

Splitting the decade on fiscal-year-end prices and non-GAAP EPS: FY2015 to FY2020 gave a +14.9%/yr price CAGR against +18.2%/yr EPS growth, so the trailing multiple contracted 13% cumulatively. FY2020 to FY2025 gave +44.8%/yr price against +25.0%/yr EPS, with the multiple roughly doubling on top. Of the +606% cumulative non-GAAP EPS growth and +81% multiple change over the ten years, the multiple change is concentrated entirely in 2021–2023 and has been unwinding since.

The 2024–2025 drawdown is the one that explains this stock. It is the deepest of the decade and it happened while revenue grew 45% in FY2025 and non-GAAP EPS grew 86%. The price declined for 343 days into the fastest earnings growth in the company's history. The re-rating produced it: the monthly forward multiple went from its series peak of 55.8x on 29 March 2024 to 26.6x on 29 August 2025, three weeks after ATTAIN-1, and to a post-2014 series low of 24.9x on 30 April 2026. From the 8 August 2025 close of $625.65 to 28 July 2026 the stock is +95% in 354 days and sits 1.2% below its all-time closing high.

Quarter Reaction What the market reacted to
2023:Q2 +14.9% Not the +5.8% EPS beat. Mounjaro US revenue reached $960M with paid-script share up from ~55% to ~67%, and FY2023 revenue guidance was raised $2.2bn to $33.4–33.9bn. About $1.5bn of the raise was the Baqsimi and olanzapine rights sales, so roughly $700M was underlying

2024:Q3 (6.3)% The only EPS miss in twelve quarters and the only quarter where revenue growth decelerated hard. Management attributed it to a wholesaler channel-inventory decrease worth "mid-single digits as a percentage of aggregate use sales," and cut the top of the FY range
2025:Q1 (11.7)% An EPS beat with a guidance cut. Revenue and performance-margin guidance were reaffirmed but non-GAAP EPS guidance was reduced by the $1.57bn Scorpion charge. The Q&A then centred on the CVS Caremark decision effective 1 July
2025:Q2 (14.1)% Nothing in the print. EPS beat by 13.4%, revenue grew 37.6%, and non-GAAP EPS guidance was raised. ATTAIN-1 top-line was released the same morning at 12.4% weight loss, below what the market had been modelling
2025:Q4 +10.3% EPS beat 12.0%, non-GAAP performance margin 47.2% (+4.2 points), and the first FY2026 guidance with price explicitly guided as a low-to-mid-teens drag, so the volume implied by the revenue number was larger than the headline
2026:Q1 +9.8% EPS beat 25.1%, revenue +55.5%, performance margin 50.0% against about 43% a year earlier, and FY2026 guidance raised $2bn at both ends of revenue and $2.00 at both ends of EPS after one quarter

Across the eleven quarters with a measurable surprise, Lilly beat consensus EPS in ten, with a mean beat of +12.4%. Mean same-session reaction was +2.3% while mean absolute reaction was 8.2%, and eight of eleven reactions exceeded ±5%. The correlation between EPS surprise and same-session reaction is 0.37, an R-squared of 0.14, so EPS surprise explains about one seventh of the reaction. Three of the ten beats produced a negative reaction, two of them double-digit; what moved the stock on those days was a Phase 3 efficacy number released alongside the results, and an acquired-IPR&D charge cutting the EPS guide plus a formulary decision. Neither is in the revenue or EPS line the previews focus on.

17. Forward model summary

Operating model only. No valuation, no multiples applied, no discount rate, no price target. Year 0 is FY2025 as filed. Revenue is never grown at a rate: the incretin franchise, which supplies four-fifths of the forecast, is built as 28-day scripts times net revenue per script for the US and outside-US separately, and everything else is built product line by product line against a dated exclusivity and pricing-event schedule.

Two gaps govern the output. Revenue equals patients times refills and Lilly discloses neither, so every script-to-patient conversion assumes twelve scripts per patient-year; and the model prices outside-US as one blended figure across roughly 90 countries with three different price-setting regimes, only one of which was decomposed.

The incretin build underneath it:

Total scripts divided by twelve gives patients continuously on therapy: 6.4M in FY2025, 12.1M in FY2026, 27.6M in FY2030 and 36.3M in FY2035 — a move from roughly 0.6% to roughly 3.6% of the "over 1 billion people" Lilly cites, against management's own framing of current penetration at about 1% and a lift to 5% as "a big lift." Base-case incretin revenue grows 168% between 2025 and 2031 while net revenue per US script declines 30% and per ex-US script declines 47%, so total scripts have to grow 4.7x for revenue to grow 2.7x.▪

Three dated events shape the path. Trulicity and Jardiance take the established cardiometabolic line from $11.7bn to $4.5bn between 2025 and 2029, with the sharpest single step in 2029 once the Boehringer collaboration has ended. The 2028 Medicare price on Verzenio holds oncology flat for a year in the middle of an otherwise compounding launch cycle. And the 2032 IRA event on tirzepatide produces the only year of declining consolidated revenue in the base case.

The FY2026 tie-out, which is the most useful validation available because FY2026 is guided and one quarter is reported:

Model, base FY2026 Company guidance (Q1 2026 release)
Revenue $84,966M $82,000–85,000M

GAAP EPS $32.34 not guided

The guidance basis excludes acquired IPR&D incurred after 31 March 2026, so the tie-out holds the charge at the $584M already booked. On that basis the model lands one cent under the low end of the guide and within $0.02 of the like-for-like consensus. The $2.19 gap between the two non-GAAP figures is the FY2026 business development Lilly has not yet announced.

The FY2026 bear runs through price rather than volume, deliberately: Q1 2026 volume of +65% is already reported and both Foundayo and the Medicare Bridge start inside the year, so a FY2026 unit shortfall is not the credible bear.

The weakest assumptions, and where the output depends on them.

  • Acquired IPR&D at $3,000M a year is the one assumption the evidence refutes rather than merely stresses. The realized three-year average is $3,330M ($3,800M, $3,280M, $2,910M), above the base and only $170M below the bear, and the pace has accelerated since: Ventyx completed and Orna, Centessa, Kelonia and Ajax agreed inside Q1 2026 alone, plus a CSL licence, with the deal tempo described as one every eight or nine days. Two independent estimates of the Q2 2026 charge alone land near $2,570M and $2,163M, so first-half 2026 is at or above the full-year base. Holding the figure flat in nominal dollars for ten years also takes it from 4.5% of revenue to 2.4% against a realized range of 4.5% to 11.1%. The evidence supports a base nearer $4,000–4,500M for FY2026–28 scaled to revenue thereafter, a bear of $6,000M or more, and a bull no lower than FY2025's realized $2,910M. At $500M a year of understatement the base case's operating income is too high by that amount and EPS by roughly $0.45 a year.
  • R&D at 19.2% of revenue in FY2030 sits below Lilly's realized intensity in every year from 2016 to 2024 — the whole bear-base-bull band of 17.6% to 22.0% does — and only FY2025 and Q1 2026 fall inside it, both the mechanical result of a revenue explosion rather than a spending decision. Management's own FY2026 commentary says R&D "will continue to accelerate," and active Phase 3 programmes went from 36 to 42 in one quarter. This is the driver the sensitivity ranks first: moving R&D and marketing intensity to their bear settings removes $10.1bn of FY2035 operating income, more than the entire incretin US volume delta. The bear should arguably sit at Lilly's own 2020–2024 average of about 25%.
  • Gross margin at 79.3% (FY2031) and 77.9% (FY2035) is probably too high. The model's own depreciation rises from $1,997M to $5,700M by FY2031; if four-fifths of that increment lands in cost of sales, depreciation alone consumes about 2.4 points of the assumed 3.7-point decline from 83.0%, leaving 1.3 points to absorb a decade in which US net revenue per script declines 30% and ex-US 47%. A bottom-up check holding the per-script input cost flat implies a consolidated gross margin nearer 77.8% by FY2031. The offsetting oral-mix benefit is directional rather than sized, because Lilly discloses no product-level cost of sales.
  • US script growth of +17.5% a year over FY2027–30 takes US scripts to 145.0M by 2030, about 12.1 million patients continuously on therapy, roughly 12% of the US obese adult population, while every disclosed access mechanism that would fund it moved the wrong way in twelve months. The demonstrated 2025–26 driver was self-pay, a consumer-discretionary exposure at $299–449 a month that the CEO calls "a bit of a wildcard." The bear at +8.9% is where the current evidence sits.
  • Ex-US script growth of +28.1% a year over FY2027–30 takes ex-US scripts to 186.8M by 2030 in markets where about 75% of the chronic-weight-management book is paid out of pocket, with the stated vehicle being orforglipron, whose only realized commercial result is that it lost the first oral round in the US by roughly eight to one on weekly prescriptions. The bear at +17.2% is the more defensible level on current evidence.
  • Ex-US price at (5.4)% a year through FY2035 is internally inconsistent with the volume assumption above it: a book whose marginal unit is sold in India and Indonesia at generic-semaglutide-adjacent prices cannot blend to $170 per 28 days. Either the volume is too high or the price is; they cannot both hold.
  • The FY2032 IRA step of (13)% is a reasonable central magnitude, but the timing is a point estimate in a run that places the event at 2031 in one place and 2032 in another. A one-year shift moves base-case FY2032 revenue by about $7.8bn, which is larger than the modelled magnitude dispersion.
  • Jardiance at $400M in FY2029 is an 84% one-year cliff resting on nothing but the 10-K's silence after 2028-12-31. Lilly and Boehringer amended the collaboration in both 2024 and 2025, booking one-time benefits of $300M and $370M plus a $200M milestone and a $250M Q1 2026 benefit; a partner that has renegotiated twice in two years is at least as likely to renegotiate again as to walk. This single line supplies most of the $3.0bn 2029 step that produces the hole in the middle of the decade.
  • Capex at $10,000M in FY2027 is well-supported at the level and the range is not: a 7% band on a line that rose 127% in two years and printed +54% year over year in Q1 2026. The bull case also assumes 43% more product on lower FY2027 capex than the base, which is the wrong sign.
  • Working-capital absorption at 30% of revenue growth rests on one year of history, and that year is distorted by a Foundayo pre-build. If the pre-build unwinds as Foundayo sells, absorption falls below the 24% bull and can go negative, which is outside the stated band entirely.
  • Impairment and restructuring at $500M a year has a one-sided distribution the range does not reflect. Lilly is "predominantly self-insured for litigation liability losses" with no reserve disclosed on two federal incretin multidistrict litigations, an affirmed qui tam judgment, the insulin-pricing multidistrict litigation and a revived 340B antitrust class action.
  • Stock-based compensation at exactly 1.0% of revenue in all three cases is a zero-width range on a line whose own ten-year record runs 0.96% to 1.84%, anchored on the record low. It is non-cash and already inside R&D and marketing, so it does not affect modelled operating income.

Two assumptions hold up on the evidence. Marketing, selling and administrative at 13.7% of revenue in FY2030 extends a long, monotone series — 30.8% (2016), 22.7% (2021), 19.1% (2024), 17.0% (2025), 14.8% (Q1 2026) — at a decelerating rate, and the most recent quarter is already only 1.1 points above the FY2030 base. Interest expense of $1,800M in FY2029 is the disclosed full run-rate of the existing stack once capitalization stops, and base-case free cash flow after dividends of $75.1bn cumulative over FY2026–29 means no new borrowing is required to get there.

The bear is not a stress test invented for the exercise. Bear revenue declines 2.2% a year for a decade to $52.3bn and EPS to $9.14 — milder than Gilead's realized hepatitis C outcome (revenue down 32% peak to trough, operating margin down 51.5 points over five years) and roughly matching Lilly's own 2011–2014 experience (revenue down 19.2% cumulatively, operating margin from 28.3% to 13.6%), applied to a book more concentrated than the Zyprexa-era book was.

Base FY2035: revenue $123,187M, operating income $52,673M, free cash flow $42,029M.

Three observations follow.

  • Operating-expense intensity outranks every revenue driver. Moving R&D and marketing to their bear settings removes $10.1bn of FY2035 operating income without touching a single unit of demand. At a 78% gross margin the cost structure is a discretionary spending decision rather than a manufacturing constraint.▪ It is also the driver on which management has given the firmest verbal commitment and the least numeric disclosure, having stopped guiding gross margin, R&D and marketing separately from the FY2024 guide onward.
  • Volume and price are close to symmetric in magnitude but not independent. Volume is bought with price, so a scenario in which volume grows at the bull rate while price declines only at the base rate is internally inconsistent with the disclosed mechanism, which is why the bull moves both together.
  • Legacy erosion barely registers by 2035 and matters enormously before 2030. In FY2029 it is the difference between the base case growing 4.9% and growing 8%.

17.4 Where this model departs from consensus

Departure Quantification
Consensus expands operating margin about 9 points from 2026 to 2031; this model holds it flat Consensus EBIT margin 44.5% to 53.9%; model 43.1% to 43.9%. On FY2031 revenue of $122,841M the difference is $12,300M of operating income
Consensus has no exclusivity event for tirzepatide; this model puts a Medicare maximum fair price into FY2032 A 13% step down in US net revenue per script removes $7.8bn of revenue and produces the only year of declining consolidated revenue in the base case
Consensus models capital intensity falling in the year the company says it will rise Consensus capex $6,965M (2026) declining to $6,188M (2028) against a model path of $9,500M and $9,600M; cumulative 2026–2028 difference $9,477M
Consensus flips operating cash conversion from 0.81x to 1.09x of net income in one year; this model gets there in five Model FY2026 operating cash flow $26,493M against a consensus-implied $32,237M
Consensus assigns Lilly essentially all of the category's incremental profit; this model prices in the ex-US concession that buys the volume Ex-US net revenue per script declines from $361 to $170 over ten years while ex-US scripts grow 10x. Consensus contains no separable price assumption beyond FY2026

Against the base rates, the base case lands at the top of the pharmaceutical revenue distribution rather than beyond it, and holds a margin that is already the sector record rather than expanding it further.▪ The one place it is more aggressive than the base rate is operating expense: it assumes Lilly decelerates below-gross-margin spending growth from a realized 16.4% a year over 2020–2025 to about 5% a year. That assumption rests on management's stated rule rather than on the record, and it is the most attackable line in the model.

17.5 What the model cannot resolve

  • Persistence and discontinuation, because revenue equals patients times refills and Lilly discloses neither.
  • The commercial-channel net price, derivable only as a residual and only if channel volumes are known, which they are not.
  • What the Medicare arrangement becomes after December 2027, given that Part D plans declined to opt in for 2027, and Jardiance after 2028-12-31, where the 10-K says nothing about terms.
  • What HHS sets as the tirzepatide maximum fair price, and in which year.
  • The oral-versus-injectable gross-margin difference, which is directional rather than sized because no product-level cost of sales exists.
  • Whether retatrutide is a niche high-BMI product or a broad one. It launches inside the forecast window at an undisclosed price, and by the account of a conference moderator the sell side models it as a niche, so a broad label is unmodelled upside sitting inside the bull volume path rather than as its own line.

18. Risks

R1. Realized price compression on the incretin franchise, accelerating. Volume growth is being purchased with price concessions on three fronts at once: the November 2025 agreements with the US government, direct-to-patient list-price cuts, and reimbursement wins outside the US bought at government-set prices. Exposure: $36,508M of FY2025 revenue and $12,822M in Q1 2026; consolidated realized price (6)% in FY2025 and (13)% in Q1 2026, with outside-US at (25)%; FY2026 guidance embeds roughly $11–14bn of revenue given up against flat price. Non-GAAP gross margin has begun to move with it — 83.6%, 83.2%, 82.6% across the last three quarters, and the reported series 82.9%, 82.5%, 81.9%. The mix is shifting toward the fastest-declining price: outside-US was 33% of FY2025 revenue and 39% in Q1 2026, growing 81% against the US at 43%▪, and management states it is "leaning in to gain reimbursement in more countries," currently reimbursed for type 2 diabetes in nine. Leading indicators: the quarterly volume/price/FX table split US against outside-US; gross margin against the "relatively stable to slightly down" guide; LillyDirect published prices; the size of prior-period rebate adjustments; the count of markets with type 2 diabetes reimbursement.

R2. The risk-bearing payers are declining the product. Part D plans did not opt in for calendar 2027; commercial employer access has been flat at about 50% of lives through a period of maximum publicity; California removed Medicaid obesity coverage for 2026; and CVS Caremark dropped Zepbound from preferred status on some plans in July 2025, which the 10-K concedes "has negatively impacted access." Exposure: the Medicare volume that does arrive comes at $245 a month with a $50 copay against roughly $550–580 of realized US net revenue per Zepbound prescription. Medicare access is mix-dilutive by construction. Leading indicators: employer opt-in percentage, disclosed only verbally; Part D plan decisions for calendar 2028, which Ricks said would be visible "as we exit '26"; self-pay share of new patient starts; state Medicaid adds and drops. Mitigation: Employer Connect, whose effect management expects only for 2027; new indications that convert obesity coverage into medical-necessity coverage; LillyDirect.

R3. Government-set Medicare prices reaching tirzepatide itself. The economically binding date is roughly 2031–2032 rather than the 2036 patent, because tirzepatide sits on the IRA's nine-year clock. Exposure: tirzepatide was 56% of FY2025 revenue and 65% of Q1 2026 revenue. The already-realized version — Jardiance at a 66% discount to its 2023 list, Trulicity and Verzenio selected for 2028 — covered $13,430M, 20.6% of FY2025 revenue. Lilly states its own expectation that more products will be selected. Leading indicators: the HHS selected-drug list published each 1 February; semaglutide's negotiated Part D price for 2027, which sets the reference point for the class; Part D volume share of Zepbound and Foundayo; the final CMS rule on the negotiation framework.

R4. Manufacturing overbuild. Capacity commitments were sized against a demand curve whose price is declining and whose payer base has just declined to fund it. Exposure: construction in progress $13,013M against gross property and equipment of $37,235M; capex $7,800M against $5,100M; total debt +$8.9bn in one year; more than $55bn of commitments since 2020; up to $10bn of take-or-pay on the narrowed population. The disclosure change is the signal: Lilly rewrote the direction of its own risk factor before the market did. A near-term version exists: an analyst described "extreme amounts of inventory preprepared" for the Foundayo launch, and another estimated from management's comments "enough doses to support at least 5 million patients for a full year." If Foundayo's curve runs below the pre-build, the result is an inventory charge rather than a lost sale. Base rate: Pfizer recorded $6,199M of COVID-19 inventory write-offs in 2023 alone, plus $3.4–5.3bn a year of asset write-offs across 2023–2025. Mitigation: management's claim that the injectable incretins share a common platform, which does not cover the separate oral solid-dose build.

R5. Single-molecule concentration, worsening. Mounjaro and Zepbound are the same molecule. 37% of revenue in FY2024, 56% in FY2025, 65% in Q1 2026; six products at 82% of FY2025 revenue against 75%. Leading indicators: the concentration sentence in each successive filing; FDA label changes for the class; the litigation dockets below.

R6. Product-liability litigation on the incretins, self-insured. Two federal multidistrict litigations against Lilly, Novo and others are consolidated in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania — one on alleged gastrointestinal injuries, one on non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy — with cases also in other federal and state courts and class petitions in Israel and Quebec, filed since August 2023 and covering Mounjaro, Trulicity and Zepbound. Exposure: not estimable from disclosure, and that is the finding. Lilly states it "cannot reasonably estimate the maximum potential exposure or the range of possible loss in excess of amounts accrued" and, critically, "due to a very restrictive market for litigation liability insurance, we are predominantly self-insured for litigation liability losses for all our currently and previously marketed products." There is no insurance backstop. Leading indicators: bellwether trial scheduling; class-certification rulings; any FDA label change adding a warning, which converts a defence into a concession.

R7. Legacy book losing exclusivity into the price reset. Four separate exclusivity or contract events land between 2026 and 2028: Trulicity ($4,276M) loses US compound patent and biologics data protection in 2027 with a government price in 2028; Verzenio ($5,723M) takes a government price in 2028 with its patent to 2031; Jardiance ($3,431M) is at a 66% discount from 2026 with the collaboration ending 31 December 2028; Taltz ($3,563M) loses US biologics data protection in 2028; and Cyramza loses both compound patent and data protection in 2026. Approximately $17.0bn, 26% of FY2025 revenue, sits inside that four-year window, and management guides Trulicity, Taltz and Verzenio to flat or declining.

R8. Gross-to-net mechanics and estimate revisions. The revenue Lilly reports is what remains after a US rebate-and-discount deduction of $62,135M in 2025 against $43,481M of US revenue. A 5% change in the consolidated liability moves revenue by approximately $897M, 1.4% of FY2025 revenue and about 4% of net income. Prior-period adjustments have run under 2% of consolidated revenue, which is up to $1.3bn either way. The live instance: Q1 2026 US price is reported at (7)% and management stated on the call it would have been (10)% without a favourable one-time adjustment — three points of price on 61% of consolidated revenue, and its dollar size is disclosed nowhere.

R9. Tariffs and China-sourced inputs. Lilly and the industry depend on China-based suppliers for "integral chemical synthesis, reagents, starting materials, and ingredients." No supplier is named and no share is quantified. What the FY2025 10-K does concede: "we may not be able to offset the burden of increased costs from tariffs and related impacts to any meaningful degree." The three-year Section 232 exemption obtained in November 2025 places the exposure at roughly 2028. Tariffs were the highest-frequency Q&A theme on the Q1 2025 call and have not been raised on a call since Q2 2025. The exemption removed the topic from the conversation; it did not remove the exposure.

R10. Competitive convergence. The franchise is defended by efficacy and by manufacturing scale, and both are attackable — efficacy by a better molecule, scale by a molecule that does not need it. Generic semaglutide entered India in 2026; Novo's CagriSema produced 22.7% weight reduction; Pfizer acquired Metsera and targets 2028 for a once-monthly injectable; Amgen's MariTide is monthly or possibly quarterly, and Lilly has disclosed no long-acting candidate beyond a Camurus collaboration. The FY2025 10-K adds China-origin competition as a named category for the first time. Lilly's own ex-US share above 53% means growth from here has to be category growth rather than share gain. Leading indicators: new-to-brand prescription share in the US and in each ex-US market; the oral class split between Foundayo and oral Wegovy; MariTide and MET-097i Phase 3 readouts.

R11. Compounding, counterfeits and the grey market. The FY2025 10-K gives the topic a standalone Item 1 subsection and names the consequence as "diversion of potential sales, and potential net price erosion for our products." A live instance: a grey market exists for retatrutide, which is not approved and whose pivotal programme is unfinished. Leading indicators: FDA drug-shortage-list status for any incretin, because mass compounding is permitted only during a declared shortage; state pharmacy board enforcement; telehealth advertised pricing against LillyDirect. The channel is unquantified in every disclosure and was not sized in this run.

R12. Pricing-practice litigation and investigations. The AMP qui tam judgment against Lilly was affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in September 2025 with rehearing denied in December, and Lilly is "assessing next steps"; the FY2025 impairment/restructuring line of $484M is described as "primarily related to a litigation charge and acquisition and integration costs" without separating them. The insulin-pricing multidistrict litigation has run since 2017 with consumers, state attorneys general, counties, municipalities, tribes, school districts, wholesalers and payers. Lilly's 340B contract-pharmacy case is on appeal to the Seventh Circuit, and the Mosaic Health antitrust class action was revived by the Second Circuit. In August 2025 a relator purported to dismiss the original Texas Medicaid Fraud Prevention Act suit covering three products and filed a second adding the State of Texas and expanding to fifteen products.

R13. Acquired IPR&D charges and effective-tax-rate volatility. $2,910M (FY2025), $3,280M (FY2024), $3,800M (FY2023); $584M in Q1 2026 against $1,572M in Q1 2025. The effective rate moves with the charge because it is largely non-deductible: 19.8% FY2025 against 16.5% FY2024, and 16.4% in Q1 2026 against 20.2%. Re-running Q1 2026 at the prior-year charge and tax rate removes $1.47 of the $5.20 EPS increase, about 28% [estimate: reported line items re-run at prior-year levels]. Neither item is operating performance, and the disclosure gives no forward visibility on either because the charge depends on deals not yet announced.

R14. Wholesaler concentration and channel-inventory volatility. Three customers stand between Lilly and every US pharmacy, each at 16–24% of consolidated revenue and 20–29% of receivables, and Lilly does not say which is which. The 10-K states directly that "incretin volume fluctuations due to channel dynamics or demand can have a disproportionate impact on our results of operations in any given period." Prior instances: Q3 2024, Q4 2024 and Q1 2025 all cite wholesaler buying patterns.

R15. EU exclusivity reform. The December 2025 agreement-in-principle would set base data protection at eight years with additional incentives made conditional, reducing the maximum available by one year. Europe was $11,558M, 17.7% of FY2025 revenue. The effect is on future launches rather than the current book.

Which risks arrive together. R1, R2 and R4 share one mechanism: growth is being bought with price, and the capital base is sized for the volume that price is buying. A single quarter in which employer opt-in reverses, Medicare Bridge uptake runs below plan, Foundayo disappoints against the pre-built inventory, and a further ex-US reimbursement win lands at a China-style discount would produce a revenue miss, a gross-margin miss and an inventory or asset charge simultaneously. The financial statements would show it as revenue growth decelerating while cost of sales as a percentage of revenue rises — the opposite of the pattern the FY2026 guide assumes. Separately, R5 and R6 are the same event from two sides: a class-wide safety signal would hit 65% of revenue, expand a self-insured mass tort with no disclosed reserve, strand a fraction of $13.0bn of construction in progress, and compromise the pipeline meant to replace tirzepatide, because Foundayo, retatrutide and eloralintide all sit in adjacent mechanism space. Lilly's own risk factor names the mechanism: "safety or efficacy concerns raised about a product in the same class... could be imputed."

Excluded as boilerplate, because no mechanism, exposure or leading indicator can be stated beyond what applies to every large pharmaceutical company: general R&D failure risk; general cybersecurity (Lilly states no incident to date has been material); general data-privacy compliance; the artificial-intelligence risk factor; general tax-law complexity; climate and sustainability reputational risk; foreign-currency translation, where Lilly discloses that a hypothetical 10% move would not be material over one year; and general third-party outsourcing except the China-supplier component captured in R9.

19. Source disclosure

Databases used. The SEC filing archive (ten 10-Ks, FY2016–FY2025, and six 10-Qs through 2026-Q1, all bootstrapped this run), 26 BamSEC earnings-call transcripts (Q3 2019 through Q1 2026) and 29 presentation transcripts (2016–2026), 11 investor decks with 614 rendered slides, nine DEF 14A proxies plus the CEO's complete Form 4 and Form 5 record from EDGAR, SEC XBRL company facts for Lilly and eleven peers, a live Bloomberg terminal for prices, consensus, fundamentals and the comparable-company table, and the CMS Medicare Part D and Medicaid Spending by Drug public files.

Gaps and failures.

  • Sell-side: none. The local digest holds 40 reports and zero pharmaceutical coverage. There is no local sell-side report on Lilly at all, so every per-analyst view in this document comes from analysts' own questions on the archived calls rather than from a published note. The bear case cannot be quoted at full strength; the one sell-rated analyst's argument, and the $850 low target 30% below the current price, could not be recovered.
  • 10-K redline diffs: not available and not bootstrapped. Lilly is not among the seeded tickers and the fallback skill was not run, so the FY2025 disclosure narrowing documented in Sections 7 and 12 is whatever this run found by hand across at least seven separate areas. The complete list of withdrawals is unknowable from the work as done.
  • Daloopa: not attempted, a scope decision rather than a source failure.
  • Web budget exhausted. The session hit its 200-call search cap partway through and the crawler returned errors throughout, leaving eight named verifications unfinished: the Lilly-versus-Novo new-prescription-share contradiction; the S&P credit rating; the May 2026 vaccine acquisition counterparties; Elanco's post-split trading record; the drivers of the 2026-02-05 and 2020-06-16 sessions; product-level detail for the Gilead and AbbVie concentration precedents; and any third-party estimate coverage.
  • Novo Nordisk's 20-F was never read, so the only marketed competitor in the franchise that is 65% of Q1 2026 revenue has no five-year revenue history in the peer tables; the 6-K route used covers FY2024–FY2025 and Q1 2025–Q1 2026 only.
  • The ten-year series was rebuilt four times rather than once, from XBRL, filings and Bloomberg, each with its own restatement-basis choices. The recorded discrepancies include XBRL disagreeing with the filed 10-K on FY2016 R&D and FY2012 pre-tax income, and Bloomberg disagreeing with both on 2016 (pension-cost basis), 2017 (Elanco basis) and 2024/2025 net debt (~$1.3bn, most likely operating-lease capitalisation). Sections 10 and 13 draw on different reconstructions that were not reconciled to each other.
  • Five of roughly 42 quarterly decks were collected. The missing Q3 2025 deck alone blocked Jaypirca's Q3 2025 figure, which is why FY2025 Jaypirca is an interpolation, and forced Ebglyss and Omvoh Q3 2025 to be taken from web coverage of that deck rather than the deck itself. Because Lilly stopped publishing a full product table in its releases and collapsed the Note 2 disaggregation in FY2025, the quarterly decks are now the only primary source for product-level revenue on eight products.
  • Both selected edge datasets were planned and never fetched. See Appendix C.

Discrepancies recorded rather than resolved. Bloomberg's 2017 revenue is on an as-reported basis including Elanco while its 2018 is on a continuing-operations basis, so its own 2018 growth rate is not meaningful and any peer table spanning that break inherits it. Bloomberg net debt exceeds the filings-derived figure by $1,302M (2024) and $1,362M (2025) with no disclosed reconciliation. Three FY2025 EPS figures circulate and none is wrong. Bloomberg's adjusted EPS consensus for FY2026 sits below its GAAP consensus, which means the fifteen-contributor adjusted panel mixes definitions, so any conclusion drawn from that field alone is unsafe for this ticker. Bloomberg never trued FY2025 to the filed actual, so growth computed off the 2025 consensus overstates CAGRs by about 0.6 points. Acquired IPR&D for 2020 and 2021 is reported at two different amounts in successive 10-Ks under a relabelled caption with no restatement note. Three different Loxo purchase prices appear in Lilly's own documents. And Lilly's Q1 2026 share of the international incretin market (53.2% by IQVIA gross revenue) and Novo's claimed 61.6% total GLP-1 volume share in International Operations both cite IQVIA on different metrics, windows and baskets, and cannot be reconciled from the disclosures.

Internal conflicts a consistency re-read could not settle. A pass over this document against its own tables left the following open. Each should be treated as a range rather than a point.

  • The five-year debt maturity wall is stated as $12,342M in Section 12, while the 2026–2030 rows of the maturity-bucket table immediately above it sum to $12,613M; the $(339)M unallocated "other long-term debt and adjustments" line does not close the gap. The $145M and $182M refinancing sensitivities are computed off the lower figure, the 3.83% weighted coupon off the higher one.
  • Cash spent on external innovation across 2017–2025 is stated as about $27.7bn in Sections 7 and 11, while the business-development column of the twelve-year uses-of-cash table sums to $28.3bn for the same years. The $925M Wisconsin parenteral site bought in 2024 is the most likely reconciling item but is not identified as excluded.
  • FY2025 invested capital appears as $60,013M in Section 3 and $61,770M in Section 13, and the same 39.7% FY2025 ROIC is presented as a core (pre-IPR&D) figure in Section 3's peer table and as an all-in figure in Section 13. The two sections rest on different reconstructions, as noted above.
  • Section 3's "US peer median ex-LLY" row does not reproduce on a single basis: gross margin (74.3%) and capex intensity (4.2%) reproduce only if Novo Nordisk is included in the median, ROIC (21.5%) and operating margin (34.8%) only if it is excluded, and the five-year revenue CAGR median of 7.6% on neither basis (6.0% either way).
  • Q4 2025 revenue is $19,292M in the quarterly tables and $19,291M both by this document's own derivation (the full year less the first three quarters) and by the sum of the five franchise lines for that quarter.
  • Zepbound's US branded-obesity total-prescription share is 66% for Q2 2025 in Appendix A, from the Q2 2025 deck, and 64% as the first of "the last four quarters" in Sections 4 and 8. The 13-week rolling series and the point-in-time series are not distinguished.
  • Weekly oral Wegovy US prescriptions are given as 207,000 by launch week 15 in mid-April 2026 and as approximately 149,000 in the week ended 26 June 2026, with the later figure described as flat-to-down sequentially. Both are [web, unverified] and come from different trackers.
  • The physician-administered chain is sized at roughly $10.8bn, 17% of FY2025 revenue, in Sections 5 and 20, while the four products named there (Kisunla, Cyramza, Erbitux, Tyvyt) total roughly $2.4bn on this document's own franchise figures. The $10.8bn is oncology plus neuroscience, which includes oral Verzenio at $5,723M.
  • The incretin unit-economics table's blended script band of ~27–35M does not equal the sum of its own rows (~26–34M), and the $366–$475 blended net revenue per script is computed off the wider band.
  • Enterprise value is $1,187,634M in the opening table (market capitalization plus filings-derived net debt) and $1,186,143M in the Section 16 comparable-company table (Bloomberg's own field). The Section 16 figure is the one behind every EV multiple quoted.
  • The increase in the rebate and discount liability during 2025 is $4,835M on the roll-forward used in Sections 1 and 13.4 ($10,313M to $15,148M) and $5,843M in Section 13.3, which is the balance-sheet line rather than the roll-forward.

Web sources. Roughly 45 distinct external sources are cited, across about 30 domains. The largest groups are company investor-relations and press-release pages (Lilly, Pfizer, Amgen, Novo Nordisk, AstraZeneca, Novartis, Roche, Eisai, Almirall, Sanofi), government and regulator sites (CMS data.cms.gov, FDA, the White House fact sheet), trade and industry press (FiercePharma, BioPharma Dive, BioSpace, pharmaphorum, Drug Channels, Precision Medicine Online), industry analysis (IQVIA, KFF), peer-reviewed literature (JAMA Network Open, JAMA Dermatology via PubMed Central), and pricing disclosure pages (Lilly's own Colorado wholesale-acquisition-cost sheets). Excerpts are in Appendix B.

Claims flagged [web, unverified], for the reader to spot-check. These are web-sourced claims whose page could not be re-fetched in this session; they are not refuted, only unconfirmed.

  1. S&P's A+ / stable senior unsecured rating (the S&P page returned an access error).
  2. The semaglutide compound-patent expiry dates by market (Canada 4 January 2026; India, China, Brazil, Mexico, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, South Africa 20 March 2026) and the Canadian rule forcing injectable generics to 35% of brand price.
  3. Weekly Foundayo and oral Wegovy US prescription counts (approximately 19,830 against approximately 149,000 in the week ended 26 June 2026).
  4. Kisunla's per-vial price schedule and the TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 completion percentages behind the roughly $37,500 lifetime revenue per patient.
  5. The May 2025 FDA clearance date and concordance figures for the first blood-based Alzheimer's diagnostic.
  6. The combined US anti-amyloid run-rate of roughly $680M and the implied ~1% penetration of the label population, including the Kisunla US quarterly split.
  7. Teva's Ajovy US share of the subcutaneous anti-CGRP class.
  8. BeOne's Brukinsa FY2025 revenue used in the BTK-class sizing.
  9. Dupixent's FY2025 and Q1 2026 revenue used in the Ebglyss comparison, and Galderma's Nemluvio FY2025 figure.
  10. That more than half of Novo's US Wegovy sales now run through self-pay channels.
  11. Sanofi's Lantus US growth in Q4 2025.
  12. Employer GLP-1 opt-in survey percentages and per-worker health-cost figures.
  13. The pharmacy acquisition cost and PBM reimbursement percentages of wholesale acquisition cost used in the value-chain table.

Estimates by method. Roughly 40 figures in this document are tagged [estimate: method], and they fall into six methods: revenue divided by a disclosed or confirmed unit price (incretin script counts, Verzenio patient-years, Taltz units, Emgality doses; about 12 figures); residual allocation of a disclosed aggregate (Olumiant, Emgality, the legacy neuroscience tail, Retevmo and the other-oncology components; about 8); mix algebra on two periods of consolidated gross margin (the incretin gross margin and its cross-check; 3); cost-build construction from published industry benchmarks (per-script and per-unit input costs; about 6); statutory or contractual arithmetic applied to disclosed dates (the IRA clock, the interest ladder, capitalized interest, the depreciation step-up; about 6); and weighting a disclosed decomposition (the regional price reconstruction, the volume implied by consensus revenue at the guided price effect; about 5). Every one has its bounds stated inline.

Claim verification. 184 of 352 eligible claims were independently re-checked under tiered sampling. High-confidence claims resting on local citations were sampled rather than exhaustively checked, and claims that were not sampled are used as written with their citations. Claims the check found overstated have been revised to what the evidence supports, and the specific corrections are visible in the text — the Q1 2026 regional price reconstruction reports about (4)% rather than a larger figure because China's price column is marked not meaningful; the Calquence comparison uses AstraZeneca's reported $3,279M; Amgen is described as still disclosing Aimovig because it does; the 2025 shareholder value award is described as the lowest in-flight mark rather than the first below its cap; the FY2024 average-above-year-end price observation covers two of twelve years rather than one; and the Metsera consideration is stated at the completed terms rather than the superseded opening bid.

Edge datasets. Two were selected for this archetype and neither was fetched; both are free coded connectors. See Appendix C.

20. What we still don't know, and the metrics that would resolve it

Unresolved material gaps.

  1. Real-world persistence and discontinuation. Lilly discloses no refill, persistence or discontinuation metric for any incretin, and management's "great persistency" is an assertion with no cohort curve behind it. A substantial published external literature exists — commercial-claims cohorts from pharmacy-benefit and health-data companies, plus peer-reviewed cohort work — and none of it was gathered in this run. Script volume equals new starts times months on therapy; if two-year persistence is materially below what twelve scripts per patient-year implies, every script count beyond FY2027 in Section 17 is wrong in the same direction. This gap bears directly on Sections 1 and 17.
  2. Geography. Outside-US revenue is 33% of the total and contains the sharpest inflection in the disclosure set, and it was analysed only for China. Europe's doubling from $4,299M to $11,558M in three years is undecomposed between Mounjaro launches, Jardiance collaboration revenue and one-time amendment benefits; Japan's absolute decline since 2020 is unexplained; and the model prices roughly 90 countries with three different price-setting regimes as one blended figure it therefore cannot validate. The November 2025 most-favoured-nation agreements link US prices to ex-US prices, so an ex-US concession is no longer contained to a third of revenue, and nobody traced that link. This gap bears on Sections 5, 6 and 17.
  3. The physician-administered chain. Kisunla, Cyramza, Erbitux and Tyvyt — roughly $10.8bn, 17% of revenue — move through Medicare Part B buy-and-bill and specialty pharmacy under a lagged average-sales-price mechanism, with diagnostic and infusion capacity as the binding constraint rather than payer coverage. No profit-pool split, lead-time analysis or bargaining-power reading exists for that chain. This gap bears on Section 5.
  4. Self-pay channel economics at the company level. A channel now taking about 45% of the largest product's US volume, and 55% of new prescriptions, bypasses the gross-to-net deduction entirely, and there is no company-level build of its revenue, gross margin (no rebate, no chargeback, no wholesaler margin, but an undisclosed fulfilment fee) or working-capital profile (cash at point of sale against a $15.1bn rebate liability on the reimbursed side). Without it, the gross-to-net trajectory cannot be attributed to channel against product.
  5. Per-segment secular trends for oncology and immunology. The growth attribution in Section 6 was run consolidated only, so the 22.5% of revenue in those two franchises has no market-growth-against-company-growth share math. The dossier therefore cannot say whether Verzenio's US plateau is a saturated fixed-duration adjuvant pool or metastatic share loss to Kisqali, or whether Taltz's decline is IL-17 class decline or share loss to Skyrizi and Bimzelx.
  6. The consensus EBIT basis. Whether Bloomberg's EBIT is struck before or after acquired IPR&D changes Section 14's headline margin comparison from +4.1 points to (0.3) points and therefore flips its sign. One check against a broker model or the estimate footnote would settle it. Flagged at the top of Section 14.
  7. The effective tax rate and Pillar Two. This run did not examine it. The FY2025 10-K names the OECD global minimum tax as a risk, the tax reconciliation includes an explicit Ireland-versus-US statutory-rate line, $12.9bn of prepaid tax sits on unrecognized intercompany profit primarily related to Ireland, the reported rate has swung between 8.3% and 20.0% in five years, and the $7.8bn-a-year US onshoring programme mechanically re-domiciles manufacturing profit into a 21% statutory jurisdiction. At Section 17's scale one point of effective rate is roughly $500M of net income, and the scenario span is about $1.5bn a year.
  8. Price elasticity. The forward case turns on it and this run did not estimate one. The MD&A discloses volume and realized price separately for consolidated, US and outside-US for ten years, which supports a bounded estimate with the launch-cohort and channel-mix contamination stated. Without one, the sign of the revenue effect of the 2026–27 price steps is undetermined.
  9. The compounded and telehealth leakage channel. The 10-K devotes a standalone Item 1 subsection to it and names the mechanism as "diversion of potential sales, and potential net price erosion," and this run did not size it. At least one public participant in that channel discloses weight-loss revenue in its own filings, so a floor is retrievable.
  10. The three May 2026 vaccine acquisitions. Counterparties, price per deal, structure and accounting treatment are unknown; they are described only in one conference transcript, and $4bn is 1.4x Lilly's entire FY2025 acquired-IPR&D charge.
  11. What happened on 1 July 2026. The Medicare obesity-access date passed 27 days before this run, and uptake, the enrolled price and which states opted in were not checked. It is a named volume driver in the model and one of the management claims pressure-tested in Section 8.
  12. The Q1 2020 transcript gap and the pre-2016 record. The earnings-call record runs Q3 2019 to Q1 2026 with Q1 2020 missing entirely, so the one prior exogenous channel-inventory shock in the window — the COVID stockpile-and-reverse quarter — cannot be observed. And the 2011–2014 patent cliff, the base rate this document leans on most, rests entirely on a Bloomberg annual series with no contemporaneous filing or management commentary behind it.
  13. What pipeline an operating-expense freeze funds. The margin path in Section 17 rests on R&D growing materially slower than revenue for a decade, and no work connects that assumption to the FY2032-plus revenue base it is supposed to produce. Lilly states it cannot report R&D by project, phase or therapeutic area, so the internal check does not exist, and the external substitute — trial starts by phase and sponsor — was planned and not fetched.

Appendix A — Investor-presentation insights and key slides

Eleven decks with 614 rendered slides were collected, running from the Q2 2021 earnings call through the June 2026 American Diabetes Association investor event. A text scan of the FY2025 10-K returns zero hits for "IQVIA", "share of market", "Performance Margin", "$55", "telehealth", "Catalyze" and "NVIDIA", and mentions LillyDirect only qualitatively. Everything below is absent from the filings in quantified form.

  • The fixed-versus-variable cost split, disclosed once and never since. 53% fixed / 47% variable in 2016 moving to 47% / 53% by 2020, attributed to the 2017 early-retirement programme, low-cost service centres and platform leverage [deck: 2021 Investment Community Meeting 2021-12-15, slide 8]. For a business whose FY2025 volume grew 50% while price declined 6%, a majority-variable cost base is a material fact about how much of incremental volume drops through, and it is the best-evidenced version of the operating-leverage argument. Informs §1.
  • The only decade-long financial frame management has published, now testable. Top-tier volume-driven growth, mid-single-digit annual net price declines on average, gross margin around 80%, and operating margin expansion with SG&A as the lever [deck: 2021 ICM, slide 26]. Three of the four were beaten; the price commitment broke by roughly 3x against FY2026 guidance of a low-to-mid-teens decline [deck: Q4 2025 2026-02-04, slide 12]. Informs §14 and §10.
  • Performance margin is a deck-and-release metric that does not exist in the 10-K, and it is the metric FY2026 guidance is set on (47.0–48.5%, raised from 46.0–47.5%) [deck: Q1 2026 2026-04-30, slides 6 and 13]. A reader working only from the 10-K will not find it. Informs §1 and §10.
  • The entire market-share dataset is deck-only. The 10-K discloses no market share at all. US incretin prescription share ran 48.7% (Dec-2024), 57.0% (Jun-2025), 60.5% (Dec-2025), 60.1% (Mar-2026) against market growth decelerating from +45% to +30% year on year over the same five quarters [decks: 43rd JPM 2025-01-14 slide 3; Q2 2025 slide 10; Q4 2025 slide 10; Q1 2026 slide 9]. Informs §4.
  • New-patient share moved first on the CVS exclusion, and total share followed two quarters later. Zepbound's US branded anti-obesity total-prescription share rose 5 points to 66% while new-to-brand share declined 6 points, which Lilly attributed explicitly to "loss of access on CVS template plans effective 7/1/25" [deck: Q2 2025, slides 9 and 10]. Only the decks publish the new-patient line. Informs §4 and §18.
  • The $55bn manufacturing programme and its 13 sites, split between an API-and-dry network and a parenteral-and-devices network, with the dollar figure appearing nowhere in the 10-K [deck: 44th JPM 2026-01-13, slide 5]. Informs §5 and §10.
  • Capital allocation, five-year against single-year, shows the composition inverting. Business development was 2.5x capex across 2017–2021 ($14.0bn against $5.5bn) and 0.53x in FY2025 ($4.1bn against $7.8bn), while the growth-to-return split held at roughly 70/30 in both periods [decks: 2021 ICM slide 10; Q4 2025 slide 11]. Physical capacity has displaced acquired science as the marginal dollar's destination. Informs §10.
  • Management's own statement that the binding constraint moved, laid out as four "from / to" transitions: single marketed product to broad portfolio, demand outpacing supply to 13 sites under construction, payer barriers to new access models, conventional pharma to a consumer platform [deck: 44th JPM 2026-01-13, slide 3]. The 10-K describes both constraints in risk-factor prose and never states the handoff. Informs §5 and §6.
  • The Foundayo launch mechanics, including the number that would falsify the market-expansion claim. Retail from 9 April, 12-plus telehealth platforms at about 35% of launch volume, access at two of three major PBMs by mid-May, and 80%-plus of prescriptions new to the incretin class [deck: Q1 2026, slide 11]. A third of launch volume routing through telehealth rather than the physician-and-PBM channel is a distribution fact the 10-K does not quantify. Informs §1 and §4.
  • The only quantified supply metric Lilly has ever published: saleable incretin doses produced in H1 2025 were 1.6x H1 2024 [deck: Q2 2025, slide 6]. Informs §5.
  • The R&D productivity claim, restated on a shifted window. "20 new medicines in 10 years (2014–2023)" became "24 NME launches from 2015–2025," so the two series cannot be chained, and the "3.5 years faster than industry from discovery to first launch" figure is footnoted to a proprietary vendor study with no public version [decks: 2021 ICM slides 34 and 43; 44th JPM slide 7]. Informs §2 and §10.
  • The answer to single-molecule concentration, in management's framing: 75%-plus of new clinical medicines sit outside incretins and amylins, mapped to named US patient populations — chronic pain 51M, elevated Lp(a) 63M, preclinical Alzheimer's 20M, early breast cancer 3M [deck: 44th JPM 2026-01-13, slide 6]. Informs §3.
  • A disclaimer that appears in the 2026 decks and not the 2025 ones. The same deck that headlines "#1 in obesity" and "#1 in diabetes" states on its safe-harbour page that these market positions "do not reflect Lilly's share of any relevant antitrust market and do not include the full set of therapeutic or other alternatives reasonably available to patients and prescribers" [deck: 2026 ADA 2026-06-06, slides 4 and 29]. Informs §4.
  • The next Investment Community Meeting is scheduled for 7 December 2026 [deck: Q1 2026, slide 20], a five-year gap since the last full investor day, spanning the entire incretin build-out.

Appendix C — External data sources

Two external datasets are registered for this company's archetype. Neither was pulled in this run, and both are free coded connectors that would have tested the run's largest structural disclosure gap and its one unverifiable management productivity claim. They are listed as a menu, not as data.

openFDA drug approvals — status: not yet pulled (available on demand). A public API over the FDA's Drugs@FDA database covering drug application approvals and submissions by sponsor over time, at as-filed cadence. It measures approval cadence by sponsor: how many new molecular entities and supplemental applications a company cleared in each year, and how that compares with named peers on identical definitions. Company resolution runs through the FDA's stored sponsor name, which is often a bare token rather than the full legal name, so the exact stored form has to be confirmed before fetching.

How it would inform this analysis. Section 2 can only state Lilly's "3.5 years faster from discovery to first launch" as an unverifiable management assertion, because the only support is a proprietary vendor study cited on Lilly's own slide with no public version. It also has to take "24 NME launches from 2015–2025" as given, which is Lilly's own tally on a window that shifted by a year in both directions from the earlier "20 in 10" framing, so the two series cannot be chained. Approvals by sponsor and year is a direct external check on the launch count and a partial one on the speed claim, and it benchmarks Lilly against Novo, Merck, AstraZeneca and Pfizer on one basis. It would strengthen Section 2's differentiation evidence and Section 4's competitive scoreboard.

clinicaltrials.gov trial starts — status: not yet pulled (available on demand). A public API over the clinicaltrials.gov registry giving annual trial-start counts by phase and lead sponsor, at as-filed cadence. Company resolution runs through the lead-sponsor name exactly as the registry spells it.

How it would inform this analysis. This is the only external measure of the thing Lilly states it cannot report. The FY2025 10-K says the company does "not have sufficiently reliable data to report on total research and development costs by project, by pre-clinical versus clinical spend, or by therapeutic category," which five separate strands of this document record as a structural gap: Section 2 cannot compute R&D productivity per platform, Section 3 cannot test the pipeline-succession claim against peers, and Section 20 flags that the margin path in Section 17 rests on R&D growing materially slower than revenue for a decade with no way to connect that assumption to the pipeline it is supposed to fund. Trial starts by phase and lead sponsor gives a physical unit for research output — how many Phase 1, Phase 2 and Phase 3 studies Lilly initiates each year against the peers doing the same — which is the closest available substitute for the disclosure the issuer does not provide. It would strengthen Section 6's growth-attribution work and Section 4's competitive scoreboard, and it would put an external number underneath Section 17's most attackable assumption.

Both are single fetch calls. When either is pulled, its series, chart, coverage window and [data: <dataset>, pull <YYYY-MM-DD>]-cited figures fold into this appendix and into the body sections named above.
